Industry News: Scientists discover a hidden gut defense that could prevent colon cancer

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1819 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A common antibody found throughout the digestive tract may provide an unexpected defense against colon cancer.
  • In a recent development, in a study published in Nature, scientists found that mice missing a type of antibody known as immunoglobulin A (IgA) developed more than twice as many colon tumors as mice with normal levels of the antibody.
  • Even more promising, when the team administered IgA orally to mice that lacked the antibody, the animals no longer revealed an elevated risk of developing tumors.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A common antibody found throughout the digestive tract may provide an unexpected defense against colon cancer. Researchers at Rockefeller University have discovered that these immune molecules help regulate the growth of cells lining the intestine, potentially preventing the uncontrolled cell division that can lead to tumors.

In a recent development, in a study published in Nature, scientists found that mice missing a type of antibody known as immunoglobulin A (IgA) developed more than twice as many colon tumors as mice with normal levels of the antibody. The researchers also uncovered how this protection works. IgA attaches to cells along the intestinal lining and helps prevent them from multiplying too rapidly.

Even more promising, when the team administered IgA orally to mice that lacked the antibody, the animals no longer revealed an elevated risk of developing tumors.

Recent findings suggest that "One intriguing aspect of this work is that it shows how a natural defense in the gut restrains the cell division that can lead to cancer," claims senior author Daniel Mucida, who leads Rockefeller's Laboratory of Mucosal Immunology. "Most cancer research focuses on trying to destroy a tumor that already exists, but what if we could intervene before tumors form?".

It has been revealed that the findings may help explain why people with IgA deficiency, a condition in which the body produces little or none of this antibody, face a greater risk of colorectal cancer. They also offer upcoming insight into how gut bacteria, immune defenses, and intestinal cells work together to influence cancer development, potentially even in people with otherwise healthy immune systems.

Why the Gut Contains So Much of This Antibody.

IgA is one of the immune system's most abundant antibodies in the digestive tract, where it provides an important early defense against potentially harmful microbes. Unlike antibodies that recognize a single specific target, IgA can interact with many different kinds of gut bacteria and even certain healthy cells belonging to the body.

It has been revealed that scientists have known for decades that the intestines contain unusually large quantities of IgA. However, the reasons for its abundance, and the full range of functions it performs, have remained incompletely understood.

Mucida's laboratory investigates how the intestine manages two essential but sometimes competing responsibilities. It must defend the body against dangerous microorganisms while allowing nutrients from food to pass into the bloodstream. Earlier research from his team has also helped explain how immune cells in the digestive tract contribute to food intolerances and allergies.

For the fresh study, Gregory Donaldson, a former postdoctoral researcher at Rockefeller who is now an assistant professor at UCLA, set out to better understand how IgA interacts with intestinal bacteria and whether those interactions might influence the development of colon cancer.

According to recent reports, "We know these antibodies bind bacteria and, by doing so, can shape the microbiome," he notes. "And because IgA deficiency, which affects about 1 in 500 people in the U.S., is linked to colorectal cancer, I wondered whether these interactions might be relevant to the disease.".

The microbiome is the community of microorganisms living in and on the body. In the intestines, these microbes perform vital functions related to digestion and immune health, but certain bacteria can also contribute to disease under the wrong conditions.

Missing Gut Antibodies More Than Doubled Colon Tumors.

In a recent development, to investigate IgA's protective effects, Donaldson compared mice that could not produce the antibody with mice that had normal IgA levels. Both groups were raised together, allowing the researchers to control for differences in food and exposure to microorganisms.

Industry observers note that the results revealed a striking difference. Animals without IgA developed substantially more colorectal tumors than their counterparts, consistent with the increased colorectal cancer risk observed in humans with IgA deficiency.

Industry observers note that the association was not limited to a single experimental setup. Researchers observed the same pattern using multiple models of colon cancer, strengthening the evidence that IgA plays a meaningful protective role.

"We found this was true for several different kinds of models of colon cancer, so that was a really convincing effect," claims Donaldson.

The team then tested whether replacing the missing antibody could reverse the effect. When mice lacking IgA received oral doses of the antibody, their increased susceptibility to colon tumors disappeared.

Industry observers note that this result suggested that IgA does more than simply accompany other protective processes in the intestine. Its presence appears to directly influence conditions that determine whether tumors develop.

Scientists Discover a Natural Brake on Cancer Cell Growth.

Recent findings suggest that to understand the mechanism behind this protection, the researchers examined epithelial cells, which form the inner lining of the intestine. These cells are particularly vital because colon cancer begins when cells in this tissue undergo changes that allow them to grow uncontrollably.

Recent findings suggest that the intestinal lining is constantly renewing itself. Older or damaged cells are replaced by fresh ones, making controlled cell division essential for keeping the digestive tract healthy. However, when the signals that regulate this process become disrupted, excessive growth can create opportunities for cancer to develop.

In mice without IgA, the researchers identified changes in gene activity associated with cell proliferation, the process through which cells divide and increase in number. Crucially, these changes appeared before any tumors became visible, suggesting that the antibody helps regulate an early step in cancer development.

"We assumed there must be some sort of receptor on the epithelial cells that was mediating this," Donaldson says.

The researchers suspected that IgA was interacting with a specific molecular structure on the surface of intestinal cells, allowing it to influence how those cells behaved.

Gabriella Lima dos Reis, the study's second author and a graduate student working in Gabriel Victora's laboratory, investigated a promising candidate called DMBT1.

Sources indicate that DMBT1 is a receptor found on the surface of epithelial cells that can bind to IgA. Previous research had connected it to several types of cancer, but scientists had not established precisely how it functions in the development of colon tumors.

How Gut Bacteria and IgA Control Tumor Formation.

Further experiments revealed that DMBT1 plays two very different roles depending on whether IgA is present.

According to recent reports, when intestinal bacteria are present, DMBT1 activates signals that encourage epithelial cells to divide. This response is part of the normal activity of the intestinal lining, which must continually replace cells to maintain its protective barrier.

IgA helps keep that growth under control. When the antibody binds to DMBT1, it restrains the receptor's activity, effectively acting as a brake on cell proliferation.

Without IgA, however, DMBT1 signaling can continue without sufficient restraint. Intestinal cells then divide more rapidly than they should, increasing the likelihood that tumors will develop.

The researchers confirmed that this excessive growth depends on several interacting factors. When gut bacteria were absent, DMBT1 signaling was disabled, or normal amounts of IgA were available, epithelial cell division remained under control.

Together, these findings reveal how a common immune molecule helps maintain the delicate balance between necessary tissue renewal and potentially dangerous overgrowth.

In a recent development, "If IgA is missing, epithelial cells that are performing their normal function -- responding to bacteria by producing new cells -- can keep dividing unchecked, leading to cancer," Mucida says. "We think this homeostatic effect is IgA's main function. This was a significant surprise.".

It has been revealed that homeostasis refers to the body's ability to maintain stable, healthy conditions despite constant changes in its environment. In this case, IgA appears to support that balance by preventing normal intestinal cell renewal from becoming excessive.

A New Possibility for Preventing Colon Cancer.

By identifying DMBT1's normal role in intestinal cells, the Rockefeller team has uncovered a potential target for future colon cancer prevention strategies.

Instead of waiting until a tumor develops and then attempting to destroy it, researchers may eventually be able to influence the biological signals that make tumors more likely to form.

In a recent development, "Based on the mechanism we discovered, perhaps we could influence epithelial cells to be less likely to develop into a tumor," Mucida indicates. "We know, for example, that having polyps increases your chances of getting colon cancer, so we think that there could be an opportunity to target this pathway after polyps are removed. Right now, there are no interventions available at that point.".

It has been revealed that colon polyps are growths that develop along the inner lining of the large intestine. Although many are harmless, some can eventually become cancerous. Removing them during a colonoscopy can reduce cancer risk, but researchers are interested in finding additional ways to prevent future tumors from developing.

The newly identified IgA and DMBT1 pathway could offer one such opportunity, although additional research is needed to determine whether targeting it would be effective and safe in humans.

Could Beneficial Gut Bacteria Help Prevent Cancer?

The discovery also raises another intriguing possibility. Certain intestinal bacteria may actively help protect against cancer by influencing how epithelial cells behave or by encouraging the production of protective antibodies.

While much of the research into the gut microbiome and cancer has focused on harmful bacteria that promote tumor formation or accelerate cancer growth, some microbes may have the opposite effect.

"What is potentially even more exciting is that there is evidence that individual species of bacteria can have really specific effects on epithelial cells as well," Donaldson notes. "A lot of research has focused on bacteria that induce tumors or can exacerbate their growth, but we have some evidence that there are bacteria that could do the opposite, just as IgA does. To that end, perhaps we could develop a probiotic supplement that induces a protective IgA response. This is all very speculative, but it's one direction that we could look towards in the future.".

Such an approach would aim to use beneficial microorganisms to stimulate the body's existing protective mechanisms rather than directly attacking cancer cells. However, the idea remains speculative, and the mouse experiments do not establish that taking IgA supplements or probiotics can prevent colon cancer in people.

For now, the findings provide a clearer picture of how the immune system and gut microbiome cooperate to maintain healthy intestinal tissue. They also suggest that some of the body's most crucial defenses against cancer may operate long before the disease becomes detectable.

Mucida adds, "Overall, there is a lot more to learn about how the dance between bacteria, antibodies, and epithelial cells in the gut works to maintain health.".

Xenogears Is Finally Getting Remastered, But Not in the Way You Think

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (789 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dualshockers

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that there are two perspectives on remasters and remakes.
  • To be fair, three Xenogears remasters are at the moment being developed by fans, each with its own codename: Weltall, Exodus, and Atlas.
  • The project could hardly be called a Xenogears remaster if it didn't include notable upgrades over the original.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that there are two perspectives on remasters and remakes. On one hand, we have those who complain whenever a developer announces a fresh one, wishing they would dedicate development efforts to bringing new IPs to life. On the other hand, we have those who rejoice and feel the nostalgia tingling whenever a game that shaped their tastes returns to the modern era. I fall into the latter camp, which is why I am extremely excited for the upcoming fanmade remaster of Xenogears.

To be fair, three Xenogears remasters are at the moment being developed by fans, each with its own codename: Weltall, Exodus, and Atlas. Today I'll discuss the Atlas remaster because it seems to be the one the fanbase is most excited about, and it already has an imminent release date of 15 December 2026. However, keep in mind that since this is not an official remaster from Square Enix, you can only legally play it if you own an original copy of Xenogears at home.

The project could hardly be called a Xenogears remaster if it didn't include notable upgrades over the original. According to the creator, Reddit user Ok-Bed3203, the entire game has been rebuilt in the Godot engine and will run directly inside it, provided you supply your own copy of the game. Fans can experience Xenogears Atlas in two distinct visual styles, dubbed Canon and HD.

It has been revealed that in Canon mode, the visuals remain faithful to the 1998 release, while incorporating technical fixes such as eliminating flickering triangles or textures, stabilizing sprites and images, and smoothing out screen fades. Meanwhile, High Definition mode introduces enhanced textures and sprites, 16:9 widescreen support (with menus, text, and FMVs preserved in their original 4:3 framing so nothing gets stretched), updated lighting and visual effects, and 3D Gears.

Both modes will support 60 FPS, 120 FPS, or your monitor's native refresh rate. They also include 2K CG cutscenes upscaled by Laichzeit (likely exclusive to HD mode, though not explicitly specified), subtitles in every language, fan translations, and quality-of-life options like text speed adjustments, quick loads, full-screen or windowed modes, and automatic pausing when running in the background.

In a recent development, after the initial release, the developers plan to add a Mods menu that lets you load custom text patches and swap images or audio files by name, along with remastered music from Xenogears' iconic soundtrack and further touch-ups to the 2K movies. The community has also suggested several additions presently under consideration, including random encounter rate toggles, a reduced-flash mode, auto-advancing dialogue, optional voice-over via the Spoken Mirror fan dub (slated to arrive alongside the Disc 2 remake), and a dedicated Android port.

Sources indicate that as you probably noticed, the developer mentioned a Disc 2 remake. That sounds like a tall order, because as anyone who played the game remembers, Xenogears features a pristine Disc 1, whereas the second disc was famously rushed after Square cut the budget before the project could be finished, which severely undermined the experience. Atlas aims to give Disc 2 the breathing room it never received. While it is not yet completely clear what that will entail or when it will arrive, it is easily the most intriguing prospect of this entire fanmade remaster.

Sources indicate that while the project looks incredible and has me thoroughly hyped, one looming question always hangs in the air these days: was this project made using AI? The developer preemptively addressed that very concern:.

According to recent reports, “About AI, since it always comes up: yes, I used AI as a tool along the way, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. But this is not a vibe-coded project. I checked every cutscene, every movement and every 16:9 margin by hand, then fixed it and compared it with the original. A huge part of the work was the boring part: tracking down the smallest glitches left over from the PS1 renderer, one by one, until they were gone. Monk work, honestly. I hope you'll feel it when you play.”.

About AI, since it always comes up: yes, I used AI as a tool along the way, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise.

So there you have it. If you want to experience or revisit Xenogears with revamped visuals, quality-of-life additions, tweaks, and technical fixes, Xenogears Atlas might just be the way to go. This Xenogears remaster launches on 15 December 2026, via Godot for PC, though you will still need your original copy to get it running. Who knows, maybe this will finally wake Square Enix up to greenlight a full-fledged official remaster, or at least sell the IP back to Tetsuya Takahashi.

Recent findings suggest that you’re probably aware that all the way back in 1963, Ford tried (unsuccessfully) to buy Ferrari from old Enzo. “Il Commendatore” quite famously used the offer to secure a better deal for himself with Fiat, angering and embarrassing “The Deuce” to the point that Ford wrote a blank check to beat Ferrari at the 24 Hours of Le Mans. While Ford achieved its goal in 1966, it seems the company still holds something of a grudge. Meet the Ford GT41, the new Hypercar that Ford is hoping will put it back on the top step at Le Mans.

See all results for used Ford for sale near 27704.

According to recent reports, the GT41 gets its name because, you guessed it, the air intake at the top of the car measures 41 inches above the ground. Well, technically, the GT41 stands at 41.7 inches tall, but Ford executives told Car and Driver that they preferred the sound of GT41 over GT41.7, and they had no interest in rounding up.

Recent findings suggest that the GT41’s power is naturally aspirated, of course; this is an American race team, after all, though it is mated to a hybrid system as required by regulations. Still, the combustion part of the equation is handled by a Coyote V-8 engine that has been bored to 5.4 liters and developed in-house by Ford Racing engineers.

According to recent reports, despite a fair amount of grandstanding about how proudly American this program is—note the American flag, eagle, football, and Statue of Liberty graphics in the livery, along with timing the reveal to take place during the Detroit Lions game on the distinctly American holiday known as Thanksgiving—Ford still won’t commit to racing the GT41 in IMSA, here in North America. The final race livery will be revealed ahead of the 2027 WEC season’s opening race in Qatar, which will take place in March.

Jack Fitzgerald’s love for cars stems from his as yet unshakable addiction to Formula 1. After a brief stint as a detailer for a local dealership group in college, he knew he needed a more permanent way to drive all the new cars he couldn’t afford and decided to pursue a career in auto writing. By hounding his college professors at the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee, he was able to travel Wisconsin seeking out stories in the auto world before landing his dream job at Car and Driver. His new goal is to delay the inevitable demise of his 2010 Volkswagen Golf.

Scientists discover a upcoming type of depression that common antidepressants struggle to treat

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (946 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A newly identified form of depression may help explain why some people struggle to find relief from commonly prescribed antidepressants.
  • The discovery emerged from an analysis of clinical and genetic information from more than 10,000 Australians with depression.
  • Recent findings suggest that circadian depression is associated with the body's 24-hour internal clock, which helps regulate when we feel awake and when we feel sleepy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A newly identified form of depression may help explain why some people struggle to find relief from commonly prescribed antidepressants. Researchers at the University of Sydney have discovered a subtype called "circadian depression," which appears to be closely connected to the body's internal biological clock.

The discovery emerged from an analysis of clinical and genetic information from more than 10,000 Australians with depression. Nearly one-quarter of the participants in the study, which focused on people with severe, recurrent or persistent depression, showed characteristics of this newly identified subtype.

Recent findings suggest that circadian depression is associated with the body's 24-hour internal clock, which helps regulate when we feel awake and when we feel sleepy. People with this form of depression tend to respond less favorably to common serotonin-based antidepressants. However, treatments that target the brain circuits involved in controlling circadian rhythms, including melatonin, melatonin-targeted antidepressants and light therapy, may offer more effective options.

Published in the British Journal of Psychiatry, the findings shed light on the genetic factors associated with this subtype and offer a possible explanation for why widely used medications such as SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) are less effective for some patients.

A Hidden Type of Depression Affecting Nearly One in Four Patients Studied.

Sources indicate that to investigate the biological differences between forms of depression, researchers examined information collected through the nationwide Australian Genetics of Depression Study. Their analysis included clinical histories and genetic data from more than 10,000 people who had experienced depression.

The researchers identified nearly 25 percent (2,604 participants) as having circadian depression. Several recognizable patterns distinguished these individuals from other people with depression.

Recent findings suggest that those with the circadian subtype were more likely to experience seasonal changes in their depression, sleep for longer periods when depressed, and wake up feeling exhausted despite spending more time in bed. They were also more likely to be night owls, meaning they naturally preferred staying awake late and waking later in the day.

The differences extended beyond sleep patterns. Depression often began earlier in life for these individuals, and their symptoms tended to be more severe (such as mania and higher levels of suicidal thoughts). Genetic analysis also revealed an increased predisposition to inflammatory and cardiovascular health problems, along with major neurodevelopmental disorders, including ADHD.

According to recent reports, first author Dr. Emiliana Tonini from the University of Sydney's Brain and Mind Center said:.

"Our research has identified circadian depression as a new subtype, affecting around a quarter of people in our study into those with severe, recurrent or persistent depression.

"Depression is not a uniform illness, and understanding the characteristics of different subtypes means that we can give people earlier access to treatments that will be most effective for them.".

Why Common Antidepressants May Be Less Effective.

One of the most key implications of the discovery involves how depression is treated.

Medications such as SSRIs and SNRIs (serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors) are generally among the first treatments offered to people diagnosed with depression. These drugs work by influencing chemical messengers in the brain that help regulate mood.

However, the researchers found that these medications tend to be less effective for people with circadian depression. Individuals with this subtype also experience more side effects, suggesting that conventional antidepressants may not be the best initial approach for everyone.

According to recent reports, because circadian depression is closely associated with the body's internal clock, therapies designed to influence that clock may be particularly useful. Light therapy, for example, uses controlled exposure to bright light to help regulate biological rhythms. Melatonin, a hormone involved in signaling when the body should prepare for sleep, and antidepressants that target melatonin pathways may also be relevant treatment options.

Co-senior author Dr. Jacob Crouse from the Brain and Mind Center explained:.

"Because circadian depression is linked to people's internal body clock, treatments targeting the circadian rhythm, such as light therapy and melatonin, may be much more relevant, and clinicians should reach for these much earlier in people with this presentation.

"For those who find that antidepressants are not working for them, it is key to speak to your clinician for advice about your individual circumstances.".

A Newly introduced Approach Could Improve Depression Treatment in Young People.

Recognizing circadian depression earlier could be especially important for younger patients, who may otherwise spend valuable time trying medications that are less suited to their particular form of depression.

Professor Ian Hickie, Co-Director of the Brain and Mind Centre and a clinical psychiatrist, warned that failing to identify this subtype in young people can contribute to unsuccessful early treatments and unnecessary side effects.

The findings highlight the importance of recognizing that depression is not a single, uniform condition. Different biological mechanisms may contribute to similar symptoms, meaning that treatments effective for one person may provide much less benefit to another.

By identifying patients whose depression is closely tied to circadian rhythms, clinicians may be able to offer more targeted treatments earlier rather than relying on the same initial medication approach for everyone.

"We really want young people to receive the most appropriate treatment early in their course of illness.

"Most young people will be offered SSRIs first up, but for at least a quarter there are better circadian-focused medical and behavioral options to help treat and manage their condition.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alpina returns next year under new ownership with the newly minted BMW Alpina 7-series-based B7 (G72) and the X7-based XB7, both in internal-combustion and electric form. While the sedan will be a four-seater unless you insist on a rear bench, the SUV comes with three rows and six seats standard, according to our inside sources.

Sources indicate that naturally, BMW Alpina buyers can choose from a wealth of fancy options, such as two-tone paint, gradient colors, a mix of matte and glossy shades, a choice of different wheel designs, variable-tint windows and glass roofs, bespoke lighting scenarios, and fully automatic remote-control doors. Alpina blue and green remain the traditional trademark hues. Both models will feature a fully adjustable, comfort-oriented, specially tuned adaptive suspension. Also, in the B7, a reprogrammed ECU will permit a higher top speed of over 186 mph.

In a recent development, BMW Alpina’s model line should read like this: B7 40, B7 60 and iB7 70. The same gas-fed engines—a turbocharged 3.0-liter straight-six with around 400 horsepower and a twin-turbo 4.4-liter V-8 rated at up to 600 horsepower—will be offered in the XB7, which boasts a bigger battery and more grunt in the fully electric iXB7 Alpina 100.

See all results for new 2029 BMW Alpina B7 for sale near 33446.

What happened to the rumoured Alpina V-12, you ask? It’s still in the cards, but insiders don’t expect it to come to market anytime soon. The wait revolves around a life-cycle extension, a possible second facelift, and the late arrival of the new convergence platform dubbed CLAR Flex. But let’s start at the beginning. The current 7-series (G70), launched in 2022, was updated earlier this year and was due to be phased out in 2029, but this proposal has apparently changed. Because of financial constraints and reduced demand, it now looks like the 7 must soldier on through 2032, which would stretch its lifespan to 10 years.

It has been revealed that the follow-up, internally known as CF0, will likely be based on the CLAR Flex architecture, which reportedly offers significant weight, packaging, and cost advantages. The first model to tap this advanced matrix is said to be the next 5-series (codenamed CE0), which is scheduled to debut in 2031. CLAR Flex not only fuses pure-gas, plug-in hybrid, extended-range EVs, and fully electric elements in a superior, scalable manner, but it could also accommodate that coveted V-12 as one of the group’s few remaining upmarket unique selling points.

The Alpina brand releases next year, so by 2028, all markets should be able to sell all versions of both models. In terms of volume, we’re still talking low five figures here. Come 2029, the marque could do with an image boost for what’s next, which will almost certainly be at least one more latest product.

See all results for newly introduced 2029 BMW Alpina B7 for sale near 33446.

Sources indicate that to keep up the interest, those in the know predict that the two-door Vision BMW Alpina concept shown at the Villa d’Este earlier this year will be marketed in small numbers at a lofty tariff. Like the BMW Skytop and Speedtop few-offs, the bespoke Alpina four-seater would be manufactured in the coachbuilding wing of the Dingolfing plant.

At this point, anything from 75 to a couple of hundred units appears to be a realistic grand total. The Munich grapevine suggests that the head-turner designed by Max Missioni and Alex Innes will be based on a modified 7-series chassis for utmost presence and relatively generous cabin space. Although the halo car is still a work in progress, it is seen as an crucial step towards plugging the gap between BMW and Rolls-Royce with a batch of stylish individualized cars conceived to not only match but eclipse alternatives from the likes of Mercedes-Maybach.

Industry observers note that looking even deeper into the crystal ball, we can see Alpina return to its roots with a dynamic and luxurious yet subtly reduced reincarnation of the discontinued B5 midliner. Although Bovensiepen just left its mark on this segment with the B05 GT curated by Frank Stephenson and his team, only BMW has deep enough pockets and a sufficiently wide parcel shelf to offer the high-performance B5 with internal-combustion and EV powertrains in sedan and touring guise.

If they put their mind to it, the Alpinists could even extend the portfolio with an XB5, which was off limits for the previous keepers of the brand. If it gets the nod, the fresh B5 would, of course, also be based on CLAR Flex, which automatically puts the launch date back to 2031, at the earliest. Since the B05 GT costs close to the equivalent of roughly $220,000 before options, a B5 could be an attainable stepping stone for those who cannot quite afford the B7. On the other hand, a B3 is too small, not sufficiently prestigious, and not profitable enough. If it happens at all, we can only imagine it as very low-volume.

Although I was born the only son of an ornithologist and a postal clerk, it was clear from the beginning that birdwatching and stamp collecting were not my thing. Had I known that God wanted me to grow to 6’8", I also would have ruled out anything to do with cars, which are to blame for a couple of slipped discs, a torn ligament, and that stupid stooped posture behind the wheel. While working as a keeper in the Aberdeen Zoo, smuggling cheap cigarettes from Yugoslavia to Germany, and an embarrassing interlude with an amateur drama group also failed to yield fulfillment, driving and writing about cars became a much better option. And it still is now, many years later, as I approach my 70th birthday. I love every aspect of my job except long-haul travel on lousy airlines, and I hope it indicates.

Fresh mobile picks you should give a go this week.

Sources indicate that who doesn't love new games? We certainly do - there's just something about the exhilaration of a new title you can't wait to dive into, as the loading screen pops up and you enter a brave new world.

Sources indicate that of course, new mobile games are a dime a dozen these days, and who has the time to scour the iPhone, iPad and/or Android stores to catch the latest title that drops? Fret not - we've gathered a quick list of 5 new mobile games you should try this week, whether that's an undiscovered indie gem or a high-profile AAA masterpiece.

Sources indicate that my social calendar is actually starting to fill up with holiday get-togethers as early as now - and what better way to spice things up than with good ol' party games? Instead of the usual, Suits & Stallions is offering what looks to be a classier way for everyone to spend the time, though, as it foregoes the chaos in favour of some museum-y vibes.

It's all about horse racing, by the way, as you and your friends will take your picks and try to cross a grid-based board ahead of everyone else. As you might expect, there's trickery and treachery afoot, as you can sabotage your pals to win - and that's the true test of friendship, isn't it?

Download now! Suits & Stallions.

It has been revealed that escape rooms offer a different kind of group activity for some social gatherings, but for Escape the Baby Alarm, it switches up the escape room formula and adds a humorous, albeit truly heartwarming, touch in the form of young motherhood. The charming puzzler's hand-drawn visuals make it even more charming, and especially so once you learn that it's all inspired by the developer's own life experience.

According to recent reports, you'll go through the ups and downs of parenthood across 17 chapters, with 38 puzzles to solve and a lovely soundtrack to boot. If you're curious about how it all plays, Jupiter's review should give you an idea!

Industry observers note that download now! Escape the Baby Alarm.

Sources indicate that fishing has always been a staple of RPGs, but who claims it should be limited to mini-games alone? Apparently not Snapbreak, as Fishing Inc will have you fishing all day to grow your pixel-art collection.

I gave this a go when it was in early access, and the gameplay loop is as you'd expect - you tap to catch fish, then you sell remarked fish to earn money. You then use earned money to buy upgrades for your rod and better boosts for your skill tree. There's a "Perfect Catch" bar you need to tap for an even better haul, all so you can fill up your lovely collection of fishy friends.

I feel like this is one of the most unhinged concepts I've ever encountered, and that's not at all a bad thing! Everything is Crab is essentially a Survivors-like where you consume all kinds of creatures to evolve - perhaps into a crab-like creature, or perhaps not. It's all about tinkering around with the evolutionary chain to create tons and tons of combinations - and yes, there's a LOT.

There are more than 160 different abilities to experiment with across this quirky roguelite, so the only limit is your imagination!

Download now! Everything is Crab.

Thankfully, you've got your trusty crocodile bestie named Yeti to help you on your journey, along with a variety of guns and abilities to level up. And if all that action hasn't gotten your interest piqued yet, then the talking crocodile most definitely will.

10 Fighting Games That Totally Reinvent Themselves Halfway Through

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1573 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dualshockers

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I am a full-time fighting game enthusiast.
  • In a recent development, having played countless fighting games over the years, a handful stand out for how dramatically they shift their rules, mechanics, or entire structure mid-match, mid-mode, or halfway through a campaign.
  • Recent findings suggest that I grew up alongside Goku and his friends, sinking hundreds of hours into every Dragon Ball game on the PlayStation 2 and PS4.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I am a full-time fighting game enthusiast. I thrive on those intense, white-knuckle matches that push my skills to the limit—even when I have to retry a tough fight over and over. Honestly, half the magic lies in that process of adapting until you finally break through the wall. Beyond pure mechanics, though, I have a special soft spot for titles that refuse to stay boxed in, introducing new rules and systems as you progress until they practically reinvent themselves halfway through.

In a recent development, having played countless fighting games over the years, a handful stand out for how dramatically they shift their rules, mechanics, or entire structure mid-match, mid-mode, or halfway through a campaign. They genuinely caught me off guard when I first played them, keeping the experience fresh instead of letting it settle into a predictable loop. Here are 10 fighting games that pull off that kind of reinvention, ranked from the cleverest twists to the most radical genre-bending shifts.

Recent findings suggest that I grew up alongside Goku and his friends, sinking hundreds of hours into every Dragon Ball game on the PlayStation 2 and PS4. Naturally, I nearly teared up with excitement when Dragon Ball: Sparking! ZERO was declared—and once I finally got my hands on it, the combat immediately won me over, recapturing the spirit of Dragon Ball Z: Budokai Tenkaichi 3 with sharper visuals and an expanded roster.

Recent findings suggest that as I dove deeper into its Episode Battle campaign, however, I realized it wasn't just retreading familiar manga and anime arcs. By fulfilling specific hidden objectives mid-fight—like defeating an opponent within a strict time limit or making an unexpected choice—you unlock Sparking! Episodes, which act as full-fledged "What If?" timelines that rewrite the rest of that character's campaign. Seeing the story branch off into uncharted territory made clearing the main mode feel far more exciting than simply replaying the same plot beats we all know by heart.

I have been a die-hard fan of Jin Kazama's saga ever since I first booted up Tekken 3 on the original PlayStation, and I've played nearly every entry since—including Tekken 7 on PS4 (following its 2015 arcade debut). Beyond bringing an expanded roster and memorable newcomers to the table, it also shook up the formula halfway through its main story campaign to give the climax far more dramatic weight.

Throughout the first half of The Mishima Saga, the game sticks to the series' classic blueprint: straightforward one-on-one bouts fought under standard Tekken rules. Once Heihachi reclaims the Mishima Zaibatsu in the second half, though, the campaign throws traditional tournament rules out the window in favor of boss encounters featuring super armor phases, special EX and Rage meters, health regeneration, and mid-fight Quick-Time Events that turn battles into cinematic spectacles. Those mechanics completely changed how I approached the late-game fights, forcing me to play much more defensively so I wouldn't enter the next phase with a depleted health bar.

Mortal Kombat is another legendary franchise that has delivered decades of over-the-top violence, though narrative fatigue and identity issues eventually pushed NetherRealm Studios to hit the reset button with Mortal Kombat 1.

Sources indicate that I placed Mortal Kombat 1 here because of how dramatically it flips both its narrative tone and its opponent design in the final stretch of its Story Mode. Across the first 14 chapters, the campaign presents a relatively grounded reboot centered on martial arts tournaments and political intrigue within Liu Kang's New Era.

According to recent reports, once the story reaches its climax at the Pyramid of Argus, however, the multiverse blows wide open and pits you against procedurally generated hybrid fighters that mash up the appearances, special moves, and Fatalities of two different characters into one. Facing off against unpredictable fusions completely changes how you read opponents on the fly, turning the finale into a chaotic, anything-goes brawl.

Sources indicate that another absolute favorite from my old PS2 days—and one I would love to see get a proper remake or sequel—is Def Jam: Fight for NY. It let you build your own custom brawler and drop straight into a gritty turf war packed with betrayals, brutal environmental knockouts, and some of the biggest hip-hop icons of the era.

According to recent reports, what really hooked me in its Story Mode was how your moveset evolves halfway through the climb. You start by creating your fighter and picking a single base discipline from five options: Martial Arts, Wrestling, Submissions, Kickboxing, or Streetfighting. Later on, by training at Stapleton Athletics gym, you unlock the ability to buy and fuse up to three distinct fighting styles onto your character—completely rewriting your combo strings, counters, and Blazin' finishers depending on the exact styles you combine.

According to recent reports, you can't talk about standout modern fighting games without bringing up Street Fighter 6, a title I have easily poured dozens of hours into. Much like the other entries on this list, its single-player journey gradually reinvents itself into something far wilder than its opening hours suggest.

In a recent development, early on in World Tour, you control a rookie avatar roaming Metro City with a bare-bones moveset while learning the fundamentals of the Drive System. Once you travel to Nayshall and start training under multiple Masters from the main roster, however, the mode opens up into a full-blown hybrid moveset sandbox. Before long, you can mix and match special moves from completely incompatible archetypes—pairing Ryu's Hadoken with Zangief's Spinning Piledriver and Chun-Li's kicks—exclusively within World Tour and the Battle Hub.

It has been revealed that unlike most games on this list, Nidhogg reinvents its genre dynamically in the middle of every single match. Each bout begins in the center of the stage as a tense, minimalist one-on-one fencing duel where spacing, blade height, and timely disarms mean everything.

The moment one player scores a kill, though, the game instantly mutates from a methodical duel into a frantic obstacle-course platformer. The winner has to sprint across multiple screens toward their goal while the defeated player repeatedly respawns ahead to stop them using any dirty trick available—from dive kicks to throwing their sword—flipping attacker and defender roles back and forth until someone finally reaches the end to be devoured by the giant Nidhogg worm.

Industry observers note that as we climb closer to the top spot, the mid-game transformations become much more drastic. At its core, For Honor is built around its Art of Battle directional guard system, demanding careful reads in close-quarters melee duels—and in its large-scale Breach mode, the first two phases revolve around escorting or halting a battering ram.

Recent findings suggest that introduced with the Marching Fire expansion in October 2018, Breach completely changes its structure once the ram breaks through both gates. At that point, the ram disappears and the match transforms into an asymmetrical raid with limited respawn tickets, forcing the attacking team to coordinate and take down an AI-controlled Commander with massive health and area-of-effect attacks while defenders fight to keep him alive—turning tactical skirmishes into a high-stakes team raid.

According to recent reports, originally released in arcades in 1996 before finally reaching modern consoles and PC in 2022 via Capcom Fighting Collection, although it's one of those games from the Japanese company that desperately needs a remake. Red Earth (known as Warzard in Japan) took a wildly unconventional approach to the genre. Rather than pitting you against a traditional lineup of rival fighters, it built its main Quest Mode around full-fledged RPG progression.

It kicks off like a classic Capcom 2D fighter with a striking dark-fantasy aesthetic, letting you choose from four heroes, before swiftly shifting into a boss-rush RPG. As you clear battles, your character earns experience, levels up, unlocks newly introduced special moves, and picks up elemental orbs and weapons off the ground to survive multi-phase encounters against towering monsters that mutate and change their attack patterns mid-fight.

Sources indicate that super Smash Bros. Brawl remains a beloved favorite for many fans, and its main campaign pulled off a full-blown genre switch in its second act. Throughout the first half of The Subspace Emissary, the mode plays like a linear, side-scrolling beat 'em up broken into distinct stages with rotating pairs of heroes—a straightforward formula I genuinely enjoyed.

However, once the roster finally unites in Subspace and suffers a crushing defeat at the hands of Tabuu, the entire mode transforms into The Great Maze. Suddenly, those linear stages give way to a massive, interconnected, non-linear Metroidvania-style map where you command the entire unlocked roster, rescue captured trophies, and backtrack through merged zones to rematch bosses—a sudden shift in structure that completely caught me off guard back in the day.

When it comes to fighting games that radically reinvent themselves halfway through, Soulcalibur III takes the crown. On the surface, it serves as the direct follow-up to Soulcalibur II's fast-paced, 3D weapon-based combat built around smooth 8-Way Run movement—familiar territory for anyone who loved the series on PlayStation 2.

Inside its signature Chronicles of the Sword campaign, however, the game fuses traditional one-on-one weapon duels with a real-time strategy game. You command squads across a tactical map, capture strongholds, and level up custom-built units—and by the second half of the campaign, early small-scale skirmishes escalate into complex, multi-front sieges against iconic series veterans and high-level bosses that test both your strategic planning and your blade skills.

Industry observers note that infinity Nikki, the free-to-play, open-world dress-up RPG, has delivered yet another massive content drop in the form of Chromatic Beings Everbright. The latest revision brings the game up to version 2.2, and introduces a newly introduced narrative chapter, and gameplay taking place around a festival narrative.

If you couldn’t guess already, the new theme is Bloom Festival, inspired by Chinese New Year celebrations.

Industry observers note that the big new story chapter takes place in the Infinity Nikki’s Wanxiang Realm. This deceptively serene and blissful region hides a dark secret, however. Chromafaces, the mythical inhabitants of the realm, have to embody fixed identities that dictate how they live and work.

Sources indicate that these are doled out through Character Tokens, which are used to assign roles to each individual. The story follows Nikki as she uncovers the script that runs the realm and the facade it props up. Nikki will help free Chromafaces and dispel the illusion.

It has been revealed that the Wanxiang Realm is split into three areas. Cai Ye is your typical lantern-lit district, where festivals and fireworks happen. Kongming Gorge is almost the opposite of that; a quiet and cold place. Finally, Jiuhua Pavilion literally floats above the region, and it's home to neverending music and dance.

Recent findings suggest that the other massive addition in 2.2 are the two new 5-Star Resonance Outfits with some interesting gameplay implications. Where Wanxiang Weaves Life is inspired by wuxia aesthetics, and true to its inspirations, it lets Nikki shapeshift into different Spirit Personas - and automatically collect resources in her vicinity.

Sources indicate that chroma's Mortal Heart, on the other hand, allows Nikki to fly around the Wanxiang Realm, drawing on the power of the Celestial Deer. This outfit also uses Celestial Deer Vision to automatically ping and mark treasure chests around her.

You can also look forward to Nefarious Shadows, a new Ability Outfit, which lets Nikki see through disguises, and reveals hidden paths in the world.

As with every major update, of course, there are themed activities and limited-time events throughout. Hotpot House is a cooking minigame where you attempt to run the eponymous restaurant, whereas Flavor Frenzy is series of platforming challenges that tasks you with gathering ingredients. Fortune Mahjong is a little more straightforward, with support for solo and multiplayer play.

If you’re jumping back into the game soon, be sure to hit up our Infinity Nikki codes page for some freebies.

#156503. Newly introduced gum disease treatment kills bad bacteria while sparing the good

Newly introduced gum disease treatment kills bad bacteria while sparing the good

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1138 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that researchers in Japan have developed a promising new treatment for gum disease that kills harmful bacteria while leaving beneficial microbes unharmed.
  • According to recent reports, developed by scientists at Nagoya University, the treatment combines antibodies obtained from egg yolks with near-infrared light.
  • Why Conventional Gum Disease Treatments Can Cause Problems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that researchers in Japan have developed a promising new treatment for gum disease that kills harmful bacteria while leaving beneficial microbes unharmed. Unlike conventional approaches that can eliminate both good and bad bacteria, the new therapy is designed to target specific microbes responsible for damaging gums and the bone that supports teeth.

According to recent reports, developed by scientists at Nagoya University, the treatment combines antibodies obtained from egg yolks with near-infrared light. Early experiments in human cell cultures and mice suggest that it could offer a more precise way to combat periodontitis, a serious form of gum disease that can eventually lead to tooth loss. The findings were published in the Journal of Translational Medicine.

Why Conventional Gum Disease Treatments Can Cause Problems.

It has been revealed that the human mouth contains a complex community of microorganisms, many of which play vital roles in maintaining oral health. Problems can arise when harmful bacteria multiply and disturb this delicate balance.

One particularly troublesome species is Porphyromonas gingivalis (P. gingivalis), which scientists classify as a keystone pathogen. This means it can have an outsized influence on the surrounding microbial community, even when it is not especially abundant. By promoting inflammation and disrupting the normal balance of oral bacteria, it can contribute to the destruction of the bone that holds teeth in place.

In a recent development, treating periodontitis often involves eliminating the bacteria responsible for the infection. However, some existing antimicrobial treatments do not distinguish between harmful organisms and microbes that help maintain a healthy mouth.

It has been revealed that "Current treatments for periodontitis, including antibiotics and antimicrobial photodynamic therapy (aPDT), eliminate both pathogenic and beneficial oral bacteria," mentioned Kazuhide Sato, one of the corresponding authors and a lecturer at Nagoya University. "These approaches often disrupt the entire oral microbial ecosystem and can also release lipopolysaccharide (LPS), an endotoxin that may exacerbate inflammation.".

Scientists Adapt Cancer Therapy to Target Gum Disease Bacteria.

To overcome these limitations, the Nagoya University team turned to a technology originally designed to treat cancer. Known as near-infrared photoimmunotherapy, it uses antibodies linked to a light-sensitive dye to recognize specific targets. Once the compound attaches to its intended target, exposure to near-infrared light activates the dye and produces a damaging effect.

The researchers adapted this strategy to attack P. gingivalis without unnecessarily disturbing other oral bacteria. Their approach relies on IgY, a type of antibody collected from the egg yolks of hens that have been immunized against the pathogen.

Egg yolk antibodies offer a practical advantage because they can be produced in large quantities at relatively low cost. This could make them an attractive option for developing targeted treatments that are affordable and scalable.

In a recent development, the resulting technology, called near-infrared photo-antibacterial targeting therapy (NIR-PAT²), was developed by researchers at Nagoya University Graduate School of Medicine. The team included first author Hiroshi Maruyama, Professor Hideharu Hibi, and corresponding authors Sato and Kiyoshi Sakai.

Recent findings suggest that to determine whether the treatment could destroy harmful bacteria while protecting healthy tissue, the researchers tested it in human cell cultures and mice. They also compared its effects with those of conventional antimicrobial therapies.

Light-Activated Antibodies Destroy Harmful Bacteria.

Laboratory experiments demonstrated that the antibody and dye combination attached specifically to P. gingivalis. Other bacterial species and healthy human gum cells were left unaffected.

When the researchers illuminated the targeted bacteria with near-infrared light, the activated dye damaged their outer membranes, ultimately killing them.

Microscopic examination revealed an important difference between this technique and conventional antimicrobial light therapy. Bacteria exposed to the latest treatment developed tiny openings in their membranes but largely maintained their overall shape. By contrast, conventional antimicrobial photodynamic therapy caused the bacteria to break apart completely.

The distinction matters because destroying bacterial cells can release substances that contribute to inflammation. Preserving the overall structure of the targeted bacteria, even after killing them, could help limit this unwanted effect.

The researchers also examined how the treatments affected healthy human gum cells. Their targeted therapy caused no detectable harm to these cells, while conventional antimicrobial photodynamic therapy produced cellular damage and slowed healing.

Latest Treatment Reduces Bone Loss in Mice.

The team next investigated whether these laboratory findings would translate into meaningful improvements in gum disease.

In mice with periodontitis, the experimental therapy significantly reduced the loss of alveolar bone, the part of the jawbone that surrounds and supports teeth. Preventing this type of bone deterioration is especially notable because advanced periodontitis can loosen teeth and eventually cause them to fall out.

Analysis of the animals' saliva revealed another encouraging result. The treatment reduced P. gingivalis while preserving beneficial Streptococcus bacteria, helping maintain a healthier balance of microorganisms in the mouth.

Conventional antibiotics and antimicrobial photodynamic therapy, on the other hand, eliminated both harmful and beneficial bacteria in the experiments, causing broader disruption to the oral microbial community.

"Results demonstrated that, unlike antibiotics or standard light therapy, this approach selectively removes the primary pathogenic species while preserving the remainder of the oral bacterial community," Sato noted.

Together, the findings suggest that targeting individual disease-causing bacteria could help control gum disease while avoiding some of the unintended consequences of broader antimicrobial treatments.

AI Could Help Develop More Precise Gum Disease Treatments.

Recent findings suggest that although the early results are promising, the researchers recognize that periodontitis is a complex disease involving multiple bacterial species. Eliminating P. gingivalis alone may not be sufficient to treat every case.

To address this challenge, the team prepares to use artificial intelligence (AI) to examine publicly available information about oral bacteria. By identifying other important microorganisms and studying how different species interact, they hope to uncover additional targets for future therapies.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers also see potential implications beyond oral health. Periodontitis has been linked to several other medical conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis and diabetes.

Recent findings suggest that understanding the relationships between oral bacteria and these conditions could eventually help scientists identify which patients are most likely to benefit from specific treatments. AI analysis may play a role in making those decisions and guiding the development of more personalized approaches to gum disease.

Sources indicate that for now, the therapy remains experimental, with its effectiveness demonstrated in laboratory studies and mice rather than human clinical trials. However, the findings point toward a possible future in which treating gum disease means selectively removing harmful bacteria instead of disrupting the entire microbial community that helps keep the mouth healthy.

#156499. Where Does the Chevy Blazer SS EV Fit in Chevrolet’s SS History?

Where Does the Chevy Blazer SS EV Fit in Chevrolet’s SS History?

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1906 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Caranddriver

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, I recently spent some time driving a 2026 Chevy Blazer EV SS, and the experience got me thinking about where Chevy’s electric family hot rod fits in the history of SS-badged machines.
  • I am a self-appointed expert on which SS models rocked, and which ones should have been an RS at best (in high school, we all knew RS stood for Really Slow).
  • It has been revealed that I drove a Camaro SS 1LE at Carolina Motorsports Park for our How Fast Does Your Car Have to Be to Outrun a Cop?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, I recently spent some time driving a 2026 Chevy Blazer EV SS, and the experience got me thinking about where Chevy’s electric family hot rod fits in the history of SS-badged machines. Chevy established the Super Sport trim in the 1960s with some legendary cars (Impala, Chevelle, Camaro, Nova) and then applied it scattershot over the decades, with some latter-day SS models worthy of the heritage and others an exercise in credibility dilution.

I am a self-appointed expert on which SS models rocked, and which ones should have been an RS at best (in high school, we all knew RS stood for Really Slow). So here are my SS rankings, grouped by Worthy of the Name and Should Have Been an RS. Fun fact: One SS was both.

It has been revealed that I drove a Camaro SS 1LE at Carolina Motorsports Park for our How Fast Does Your Car Have to Be to Outrun a Cop? story. Our cop-evading candidates also included a Ferrari 488 GTB, and while the Ferrari was the quickest car of the day, the Camaro wasn’t as far behind as you might expect. It’s also possible that I just felt more comfortable pushing a Camaro than I did a Ferrari, but the SS 1LE remains the track-rat bargain of this century. I still want one.

See all results for upcoming 2026 Chevrolet Blazer for sale near 94043.

Industry observers note that one of my high school hobbies was cadging test drives at car dealerships. Maybe I should have felt bad about wasting dealers’ time, but on some level I believed that I might actually buy whatever car I was begging for a drive. And I was arriving in my IROC, which was presentable enough to imply at least some trade-in value. I drove plenty of cars—the second-generation Ford Probe GT with its frisky V-6 was a pleasant surprise—but I did get shut down whenever I exceeded the threshold of deal-signing plausibility that was assigned when I rolled onto a given lot. That’s what happened when I asked to drive a 1994 Impala SS that was in the showroom of a local car dealer. I vividly remember what the salesman told me: “If everyone drives it, nobody buys it.” Instead, he gave me the keys to a Monte Carlo SS. I was amazed that a car with a similar engine to mine (the ubiquitous Chevy 5.0) could be so much slower. “Someday, I’ll write a story about how not all Chevys deserve an SS badge,” I probably didn’t say. But let’s imagine I did. What a perceptive lad!

It has been revealed that I still haven’t driven a bubble-Caprice Impala SS. But I continue to revere them. They’re like a cop car, but cooler!

Speaking of cop-cars-but-cooler, the Chevy SS was the civilian version of the contemporary Caprice, and it was like Chevy’s version of an E39 BMW M5, complete with 415 horsepower and an available manual transmission. Of course, just right is never enough, so we had Lingenfelter Performance Engineering bolt on a supercharger before I took an SS on a multi-state investigation of the history of bootlegging. Sliding that car around on dirt roads out in moonshine country was so much fun I almost forgot I had a job to do. Which may or may not have involved bringing some things in the trunk back to Michigan. I get amnesia when I try to recall any details about that, but the SS—that I remember, and fondly. If you want one, maybe don’t wait too long, because the SS secret is out, based on what I see lurking on Bring a Trailer.

See all results for fresh 2026 Chevrolet Blazer for sale near 94043.

I’ve never driven a Chevelle SS, but when we had one in a comparison test, it sounded like it was a royal handful. A 13.81-second quarter-mile at 102 mph isn’t super quick now, but consider that the first 500 feet of that run was probably devoted to wheelspin management as the 7.4-liter, 450-hp (gross-rated) V-8 abused the primitive tires of the day.

Of the Chevelle’s brakes, Sam Posey mentioned, “While they’re working, they are predicta­ble.”.

In a recent development, the Cobalt SS was a sneaky performance car when it debuted with a supercharged, 205-hp four-cylinder in 2005, and later got a 260-hp turbocharged upgrade. Chevy also built it in naturally aspirated form (hold that thought). This was around the time when GM started to figure out the concept of handling, and the Cobalt SS’s excellent all-around performance prompted me to conjure an unlikely contest in 2006. The premise: I race against Dale Earnhardt, Jr., around a tight road course at the Charlotte Motor Speedway infield. He’d get a Cobalt SS. And I’d get a 505-hp Corvette Z06. I beat him, but not for his lack of trying—he pushed that Cobalt so hard he pitted in with gravel falling out of the left-rear wheel because his track-out lines were starting to include real estate beyond the actual track.

Then we went Corvette to Corvette, and that went how you’d expect, as evidenced by his note in my Z06 press kit: “Good luck next time. Dale Jr., 30.8 (you 32.2).”.

In a recent development, dropping a dang Corvette engine in a family SUV is usually the sort of procedure that requires an engine hoist, a wrecked C4, and a long weekend. But in 2006 Chevy did that deed at the factory, giving us the Trailblazer SS, a 395-hp SUV that hit 60 mph in 5.5 seconds and conjured the casual menace of the ‘90s Impala SS. It also had upgraded brakes and suspension, modifications that our John Phillips described as “comprehensively testosteronated”. If you like the whole Trailblazer SS deal but wish it were weirder, GM also built a Saab version, the 9-7X Aero. It was about as Swedish as apple pie at a baseball game on the Fourth of July, and remains the most powerful Saab I can think of at the moment.

Sources indicate that OK, the stopwatch doesn’t lie: the Blazer EV SS destroys its predecessors at the drag strip. The trip to 60 mph is over in 3.3 seconds, and the quarter-mile requires just 11.8 seconds. That beats an automatic 2019 Camaro SS (3.9 and 12.2 seconds for those respective runs), which itself was slightly quicker than the manual Camaro SSs we tested. On power alone—615 horsepower and 650 pound-feet of torque—the electric Blazer deserves entry to the SS club.

According to recent reports, in other ways, it’s merely casually sporty, but that’s been the SS mien in a lot of cases. I appreciate that you can get it in habanero orange, an extroverted hue that caused one of my kids to mistake it for a Lamborghini Urus for about 50 milliseconds. And, in this age of inflation, the $395 performance package is a huge bargain for the upgrades it brings: 22-inch summer tires and high-friction brake pads and rotors. Those front rotors are 15.3 inches and are grabbed by six-piston Brembo calipers. That’s legit hardware, as evidenced by its 157-foot stop from 60 mph.

In a recent development, the Blazer EV SS interior gives you some SS branding on the seats and steering wheel but otherwise looks mostly like any other Blazer EV, which is to say mostly like any other Chevy SUV. Which is fine. If I were the person at GM in charge of cost-benefit analysis, I too would opt for cruddy lower door plastic as long as I got to keep Super Cruise.

Sources indicate that the Blazer EV SS is worthy of the SS badge. Whether it’s worthy of the Blazer one is a different discussion that you can continue on your forum, K5 Freaks 4EVR.

The positive news here was that Chevy brought back a V-8-powered Impala SS that was good at doing burnouts. The bad news was that it could barely avoid doing burnouts at all times because it was front-wheel-drive. Yes, Chevy dropped a dang 303-hp LS engine in the front-drive Impala of the day, resulting in torque steer that made every ditch a possibility. Our own Tony Quiroga described that Impala SS as a car that “gives the feeling that it’s waging war with itself”. Other observations from that review:.

-“Keeping an 18-year-old platform competitive is not an insubstantial task.”.

-“Dive, squat, and roll control could be described as nautical.”.

-On the skidpad, “The Impala leaned over far enough to be included in Who's Who in Body Roll.”.

Industry observers note that -“Impressed by the 154-mph top speed? Driving the SS at that speed is scary enough to be a stunt on NBC's Fear Factor.”.

-“The front-strut suspension crashes over pavement imperfections as if someone had overlooked the advantages of bushings.”.

At the time, my wife had an Impala as a manufacturer car. She was a pharma sales rep for Johnson & Johnson, and her trunk was always full of Tylenol PM and K-Y Jelly. It would have been funny if she ever got pulled over and searched. Also, the second “A” of the trunk badge fell off, so we fondly referred to her car as the Impal. That was the right assignment for that era of Impala.

It has been revealed that during the early-2000s hot-truck heyday, there were some wicked creations. Ford noted, “Let’s put a 380-hp supercharged V-8 in a regular-cab two-wheel-drive F-150, call it the Lightning and do some huge burnouts.” Over at Dodge, they said, “Let’s drop a 500-hp Viper V-10 in a regular-cab, two-wheel-drive Ram, call it the SRT-10 and do some even huger burnouts.” When Chevy got in on the game, it said, “Let’s build a Silverado with an extended cab, all-wheel-drive, and 345 hp. We’ll call it the SS, and it won’t do burnouts.” Eventually Chevy built a rear-drive version, but the Silverado SS still got noogies and purple nurples at recess from the Dodge and Ford.

Sources indicate that we mentioned the Maxx itself was “a runty-looking cross between a family sedan and an ice chest,” and the SS treatment didn’t do a whole lot to energize that off-putting shape. The Maxx SS was powered by an iron-block pushrod V-6 that made all of 240 horsepower, sloshed to the front wheels by a four-speed automatic. It hit 60 mph in 6.9 seconds and topped out at a governed 115 mph. This Malibu Maxx didn’t need to be called an SS. In fact, this Malibu Maxx didn’t need to be at all. It reminded me of when I bought reflective mailbox lettering decals and made my parents’ rusty 1989 Subaru DL wagon the DL SS.

In a recent development, how is the Cobalt SS on both the worthy list and the SS trash pile? Because for two years, Chevy offered a naturally aspirated version that wheezed out just 170 horsepower. (The good version was formally named the Cobalt SS Supercharged.) Chevy itself got embarrassed by this SS’s half-heartedness and renamed it the Cobalt Sport after two years, proving that even pre-bankruptcy GM had limits to its cynicism. Happily, no subsequent SS stooped to that level, and hopefully none ever will.

Ezra Dyer is a Car and Driver senior editor and columnist. He's now based in North Carolina but still remembers how to turn right. He owns a 2009 GEM e4 and once drove 206 mph. Those facts are mutually exclusive.

Zenless Zone Zero’s latest Special Program has delivered a tonne of information about the game’s major upcoming update, Version 2.6. This latest addition kicks off celebrations in Newly introduced Eridu, and it’s dubbed Encore for an Old Dream.

Version 2.6 is not far off, either, arriving in ZZZ on February 6 - exactly one week from today. Encore for an Old Dream is something of an in-between story that takes place after the end of Season 2.

The narrative of 2.6 sees the Proxies’ return to Sixth Street for Upcoming Eridu's annual Gilded Carrot Day. At the centre of the celebrations is the debut of idol group Angels of Delusion at the 404 Error music venue, but not all is as it seems.

Industry observers note that the story follows the Proxies getting invited backstage to support the group, which also includes helping them set up practice schedules, organise events and manage social media activities. There’s a rhythm minigame as part of that, along with newly introduced maps and mechanics for Marcel Adventure.

Sources indicate that angels of Delusion is also the group that the two fresh Agents being introduced in this revision belong to. Members of the same group are capable of performing coordinated attacks. The new arrivals are Sunna and Aria.

Sunna is a an S-Rank Physical Support Agent who specialises in boosting teammates using Attack and Anomaly. Her Ultimate sees her pull out a giant hammer to land heavy damage, and bring teammates into combat using Quick Assist. Sunna’s companion, Bubblegum, can cast Cat's Gaze on enemies, marking them for detonation. Bubblegum can also buff the squad’s attack.

Sources indicate that aria is the other upcoming arrival, the group’s lead vocalist who can shift between two forms, idol projection and construct. Aria is an Ether Anomaly Agent who also deals high burst damage, specifically against enemies who suffer from any Attribute Anomalies.

Sunna and Aria also benefit from the support of the amusingly named Bangboo Biggest Fan, a fan club president who can heal them over time, and boost the squad’s Attack any time two or more Angels of Delusion members are present.

Version 2.6’s S-Rank re-runs are Yixuan (Auric Ink - Rupture), and Yuzuha (Physical - Support), who you can look forward to as part of the banners.

Sources indicate that version 2.6 will also expand Hollow Zero with a new game mode, Operation Matrix. The mode offers themed stages that rotate weekly, each offering new mechanics. You can now also Sweep in Hollow Zero.

According to recent reports, beyond all the celebrations, this upgrade also brings combat kit overhauls to a couple of older S-Rank characters, Lycaon and Harumasa. You can look forward to multiple limited-time events, too, including one where you can earn a latest outfit for Pan Yinhu.

The big event is naturally going to be themed around Gilded Carrot Day, and it actually starts today. There’s the usual run of login rewards (about 3,300 Polychromes), as well as daily activities. Yet another login event - Gilded Surprise, Wonderful Boo-ns - will be available February 14-23, offering daily draws from a pool of 4 billion Polychrome.

As always, there’s no reason not to catch up on the latest set of Zenless Zone Zero codes for some free in-game items.
