💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, do you think you have a good relationship?
  • Grand Theft Auto 6 puts a massive emphasis on the relationship between Jason and Lucia, with it being a key part of the story.
  • They can trust each other, and they will put their lives on the line to keep one another safe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, do you think you have a good relationship? Do you and your partner get along, and are you both happy? Do you have trust, and are you both still making each other laugh? If you are iffy on any of those questions, Lucia and Jason may just have a better relationship than you.

Grand Theft Auto 6 puts a massive emphasis on the relationship between Jason and Lucia, with it being a key part of the story. From the very start of the game, you need to put them first if you want them to have a strong connection.

Well, their relationship is good. They can trust each other, and they will put their lives on the line to keep one another safe. Can you say the same?

A key part of learning about your partner is asking them questions. You need to have a sense of interest in your significant other so that they know you truly love them. Without any type of interest, you end up becoming stale.

Sources indicate that that is not a problem for Lucia and Jason, as they ask each other questions all the time. If you simply drive around the city, you will hear conversations between the two of them where Lucia will ask Jason how he ended up in the military.

According to recent reports, you will also hear Jason ask Lucia about her past, about prison, and about their son. This interest shows how much they care about each other and want to know more about one another.

Trust is a key part of any relationship. If you don’t trust the person you are with, odds are you won’t make it very long. It is one of the most core tenets of any relationship, and Jason and Lucia show that they can trust each other constantly.

They put their lives on the line every time they step out of their apartment. They are constantly dealing with drug lords, gang members, and more, so they need someone they can trust, and they can trust each other.

Both of them know that the other one has their back, and when one of them makes a strong move, the other is there to back them up.

The internet made a huge stink about not being able to cheat on Lucia as Jason. Many people kept saying they wanted to see what a relationship with Mandy would be like. It would probably be terrible, but they were interested.

However, the game not having a cheat mechanic in it just indicates the strength of Jason and Lucia’s relationship. You can’t betray Lucia. You can’t go behind her back. You are required to stay loyal, but that is also the kind of guy Jason is.

Jason wouldn’t go behind someone’s back, no, he is too good for that. He is the type of guy who would rather break it off if things weren’t going right than go behind someone’s back.

Industry observers note that if you want to get to know your partner, and you want to have a solid foundation, you need to spend quality time together doing things that you both enjoy. This can be a hobby like bowling, mini-golfing, or maybe even robbing banks.

For Jason and Lucia, you have the option to have them spend time together constantly. They are able to go for walks around Vice City, take a drive, or participate in any of the various side activities found throughout the game.

According to recent reports, this type of constant quality time is great for a relationship, and it is okay to spend time apart. After all, you can split up from each other in the game, but the quality time is there, and it builds their relationship.

Communication is everything when it comes to being in a relationship. You don’t want to keep secrets, and you always want to check in to make sure that your partner is okay. This style of communication is key to making things work.

Jason and Lucia are a model example of this. When playing as either of them, you have the option to check in with the other to see how they are doing. Your partner will also sometimes send you a text or give you a call to check in.

Sources indicate that this type of relationship works because they keep a constant line of communication. They share group chats, and they also talk about what happened when they were split up.

Industry observers note that while it isn’t necessary for you and your partner to have the same exact goals in life, it certainly does help to make things operate more smoothly. For instance, if you don’t want kids but your partner does, that can cause a rift.

Jason and Lucia don’t need to worry about this rift forming as they know exactly why they are doing what they are doing, and they have the same goals. They both want to provide for their child, and they don’t want to be criminals forever.

They are criminals now to get enough money to live a good life later on. After that, they don’t need to keep going, as they will be able to live happily as a family.

A nice thing about being in a relationship is that you have somebody you can connect with - somebody that can make you smile, laugh, and feel a range of emotions. To keep things going well, you need to keep up the humor, you need to be flirty, and you need to be playful.

Sources indicate that the relationship between Lucia and Jason in GTA 6 isn’t stale. They are consistently making each other laugh, flirting with one another, and more. They know how to make each other smile.

You can complete a job, and the two of them will joke about something, or you can make it back to the apartment, and they will be intimate. You can also relax in bed staring at your phone. There is a connection, and it is strong.

This doesn’t apply to everyone. After all, not many couples out there are actively committing crime together and bailing each other out. Jason and Lucia have a bond that is forged in fire and a hailstorm of bullets. I wish I was joking.

It has been revealed that their relationship may seem okay at first, but once you are out of chapter one, you see how Lucia goes the extra mile for Jason. She puts her life on the line for him, and he does the same in return.

Sources indicate that the two are willing to die for each other if it means that their partner stays safe. Those aren’t just words to them. Each time they go out, they are risking their lives for each other, and it highlights how madly in love they are.

Microsoft's SideWinder Strategic Commander was a failed attempt to reimagine RTS controls. 23 years later, why are some players still using it?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1512 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, PC players have been conditioned for decades to accept the keyboard-and-mouse setup for RTS games.
  • Unveiled on March 1st 2000 at Microsoft's Gamestock event, the Strategic Commander was one of three additions to their SideWinder line, with a scheduled release that October at a pricey $64.95.
  • Industry observers note that microsoft, all the while, were taking notes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, PC players have been conditioned for decades to accept the keyboard-and-mouse setup for RTS games. One hand has to handle movement and commands through a keyboard, while the other points, drags, and selects with a mouse. Peripheral makers have, usually with the addition of more buttons, made many minor variations to this time-honored arrangement, but there's only ever been one real attempt to rethink it entirely for the PC: the Microsoft SideWinder Strategic Commander.

Unveiled on March 1st 2000 at Microsoft's Gamestock event, the Strategic Commander was one of three additions to their SideWinder line, with a scheduled release that October at a pricey $64.95. At E3 later that May, Microsoft demonstrated the Strategic Commander for the first time with SimCity 3000, while promoting its potential for other such games as Diablo II, Warcraft III, and Baldur's Gate II. This was all taking place during the so-called 'Golden Age of Real-Time Strategy Games,' which spanned roughly from the mid-1990s to the mid-2000s. It was when the RTS genre was at the peak of its mainstream popularity, and we fans were devoted to mastering its intricacies in any way we could to have a competitive edge.

Industry observers note that microsoft, all the while, were taking notes. "The team conceived the Strategic Commander in the late 1990s," Carl Ledbetter - then Industrial Design Manager for Microsoft's PC Hardware Group, now Head of Design for Xbox Devices - recalls to me. "As RTS games grew in popularity, we saw an interesting opportunity to design a new physical interface around a new interaction model. The idea was for it to be used left-handed in concert with right-hand PC desktop mouse control. We wanted to enable players to perform faster with more fluidity, comfort, optimised control placement for multiple hand sizes, simplicity of set-up, and ease of programming.".

For Ledbetter and co. to realise this ambition, the Strategic Commander was designed as a unique combination of mouse, joystick, and gamepad. To manage the increasing complexities of the RTS games of the day, it came equipped with six programmable buttons, three shift buttons, and a three-position profile switch. Back then, these atypical features provided an unprecedented 72 possible key combinations across various configurations, all at the tip of our stubby little fingers. Better yet, it allowed us to toggle between three pre-configured profiles at a time, so that we could switch up our configurations on the fly depending on which stage of an RTS match we were in.

It has been revealed that on release, contemporary reviewers acknowledged its originality, with critics like ActiveWin's Julien Jay describing it as "probably the most innovative (with the GameVoice) and revolutionary" peripheral designed specifically for strategy players. Others, like Neoseeker's Arnel Lim, suggested that it might’ve gone overboard with its customisation options, saying "you won't use anywhere close to all of them," in reference to the controller's programmable key combinations. Either way, the Strategic Commander failed to supplant conventional peripherals in the hands of most RTS players, and it was discontinued in 2003. As was the rest of the original SideWinder line, owing to declining sales and the industry-wide shift toward standard M+K setups for all PC games and genres.

However, unlike so many of its Microsoft-made siblings, this was not the end for the Strategic Commander. Niche as it was, it went on to enjoy a surprisingly long post-shelf life, one that was stretched out by a dedicated cult following - and that continues to this day. But why? Why, after all these years, is this forgotten peripheral from a discontinued line maintaining such a enthusiastic fanbase, years after the industry around it had written it off as a failure?

In a recent development, the answer lies in software and OS compatibility, as much as the hardware's own appeal. Andreas Weis was the developer of one of the first unofficial patches for the Strategic Commander, allowing players to keep on using it even after the original software stopped being compatible with newer versions the Windows. By that point, the device was a decade old, and well into 'official' obsolescence, yet Weis still answered the call of the Strategic Commander's righteously frustrated - if numerically few - fans. "There was a lot of interest back in the early 2010s in software patches to keep the Strategic Commander functional when the original software for the Strategic Commander stopped working," he explains. "Customers were asking around on internet forums about how to get it to work on Windows 7 and Vista machines. Since I was studying computer science at the time, I was quite interested in reverse-engineering, and I hacked together a simple tool that would cover my use cases for the device.".

In the years that followed, other patches were released to keep the Strategic Commander operational, the most notable of which was Philip Merwarth’s Strategic Engine software in 2013. Unfortunately, they weren’t open-source. Worse was that the protocol for programming the Strategic Commander wasn’t documented anywhere online in a way that was accessible for users. This is why Weis realized that he could make a unique contribution.

In a recent development, "I polished my old prototype code for the Strategic Commander software patch and released it as a library, so that other people could use it to write their own applications for programming the tool," he notes. "As for me, I released one application that made use of the library publicly, the vJoy feeder application, which allows the device to be used with games that support joystick inputs." Curiously, Weis, by this time and like many others, had found other applications for a device with such a specific selling point, and even continues to use the Strategic Commander sparingly in 2026.

According to recent reports, "The production quality of Microsoft hardware at the time was just top-notch, and I love the design of the old SideWinder devices, which is why I did not just throw the thing out when the software stopped working," he tells me. "It was worth keeping around to find upcoming uses for it over the years, and I eventually realized that it makes quite a nice addition to a HOTAS (Hands-On Throttle And Stick) setup, where I could put actions that aren’t time-critical and don't fit well on the throttle on the Strategic Commander instead. For example, when I’m playing Elite Dangerous in VR, I’d put actions like deploying the landing gear on the Strategic Commander to free up buttons on the throttle for actions that were more relevant for combat.".

According to recent reports, when looking back at the history of Microsoft’s SideWinder line, it’s easy to call the Strategic Commander a failed experiment, given the fact that most of us are still using the same standard mouse-and-keyboard setup to play RTS games. However, the central premise behind its design philosophy was that the interface between a player and a game could be redesigned to cater to specific genre quirks, and decades following its release, it’s still maintained a coalition of loyal consumers: some RTS players who believed the Strategic Commander really pulled it off, and those found other uses for the device in other flavours of PC game. And with the problem of modern compatibility, a roadblock for so much retro hardware, bypassed by homemade patches, both camps can continue twisting and clicking their Strategic Commanders unimpeded.

Sources indicate that all the same, I wonder if it might have basked in more conventional success, had Microsoft made more forward-thinking decisions. The Strategic Commander has proven over the years that its unprecedented customisation had applications far beyond what Ledbetter’s team had envisioned, and once the popularity of RTS games settled down, other, similar click-heavy subgenres like MOBAs and Real-Time Tactics got massive as well. Would a more officially maintained, potentially refined Strategic Commander model have served those crowds? I think it might. The narrow focus on RTS games may have also hurt the device's since-demonstrated broader appeal; if Microsoft had fully capitalised on this customisation selling point by communicating its benefits to everyone, not just those playing the single most popular PC genre at the time, it could have provided the blueprint for a proper, long-lived alternative to controllers, mice, and keyboards.

Alas, gaming history is littered with revolutionary peripherals that failed to actually revolutionise the industry surrounding them. The Strategic Commander is no different, but for the fact that it’s had this surprisingly long post-shelf life - and, as a result, the opportunity for insight into what could have been done to salvage the its failures. Still, that unexpected longevity can provide come comfort to the Strategic Commander's creators, as well as its lingering customers.

In a recent development, "I think the design made sense for its time, especially with the rising popularity of RTS games," Ledbetter reflects. "Looking back, I would have liked more time to test and refine the Strategic Commander. I’m proud of what we brought to market, and I’m glad to know that it remains beloved by many players to this day.".

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Fnatic has made its first confirmed exit official as it rebuilds its LEC roster for 2027.
  • The club marked the departure with a farewell video titled “Thank You, Iván”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, fnatic has confirmed the departure of its longest-serving player, jungler Razork, who is set to join Team Heretics. With support Lospa also set to leave, the London club faces a near-total LEC roster rebuild for 2027.

Fnatic has made its first confirmed exit official as it rebuilds its LEC roster for 2027. Razork was the London club’s longest-serving player and its main playmaker. He leaves after five seasons in the jungle.

The club marked the departure with a farewell video titled “Thank You, Iván”. In it, Fnatic recalls him arriving as a young player with huge ambition. He had entered the LEC with Misfits Gaming in 2020 before moving to Fnatic in 2022. The club later extended his contract to run through 2026.

Recent findings suggest that his next stop appears to be Team Heretics. Sheep Esports reported that the 26-year-old will play alongside midlaner Jackies and support Jun. Heretics had already tried to sign him a year earlier. On that occasion it agreed a buyout with Fnatic but could not agree terms with the player.

The rebuild runs deeper than the jungle. Every Fnatic team member except Lospa was due out of contract in 2026. The support was signed until the end of 2027.

That deal will not keep him at Fnatic either. Lospa has reportedly agreed verbally to join SK Gaming for 2027. No buyout is involved in moving his contract between the two clubs. With that move, the one contract running beyond 2026 also leaves the club.

In the jungle, Yike is set to replace Razork in a 2027 line-up of Soboro, Yike, Vladi, Doggo and Labrov, according to Sheep Esports sources.

The overhaul follows a difficult year. Fnatic finished eighth in LEC 2026 Versus. It then placed seventh in Spring, which ended on 10 May. Summer brought the same finishing position.

It has been revealed that A loss to GIANTX on 30 August kept the team out of the Summer playoffs. That defeat left the club absent from Worlds for the first time since 2016.

5 years of memories. it was an honour to see you grow into the person and player you are 🧡 https://t.co/F3TWY9WZqq pic.twitter.com/K3K3EQICZ1.

— FNATIC (@FNATIC) November 17, 2026.

For the UK scene, the scale of change matters. Fnatic is one of the LEC’s best-supported clubs among British fans.

The club has also opened a search for a League of Legends General Manager. Its job advert indicates Fnatic goes into a rebuild in 2027. The latest hire will run recruitment of players, coaches and staff, including transfers and benchings, and will manage the team’s budget.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The first class, being the Paladin, is already available to play for anyone who pre-ordered the expansion, but the Warlock won’t be accessible until the expansion arrives in late April.
  • In a recent development, the Warlocks are positioned as the opposite of the Paladins, in that they don’t mind utilising forbidden knowledge, drawing on the powers of Hell itself to fight its own overlords.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Diablo 4’s segment in the big Diablo 30th Anniversary Spotlight was among the biggest, even if the reason most of us tuned in was somewhat spoiled earlier in the same livestream. Blizzard unveiled the Warlock, the second of two classes coming to the game with the upcoming Lord of Hatred expansion.

The first class, being the Paladin, is already available to play for anyone who pre-ordered the expansion, but the Warlock won’t be accessible until the expansion arrives in late April.

In a recent development, the Warlocks are positioned as the opposite of the Paladins, in that they don’t mind utilising forbidden knowledge, drawing on the powers of Hell itself to fight its own overlords. The Warlock is the edgy, antihero counterpart to the Paladin’s purity and devotion to the Light.

The livestream did not show off any Warlock gameplay, but Blizzard is planning a dedicated livestream to show off the fresh class’ gameplay, and dig deeper into its lore and abilities. That show is scheduled for March 5.

Recent findings suggest that what we did get to see was our first look at Skovos, the expansion’s fresh region. This Mediterranean-inspired location is where the new story arc will unfold, but it’s also being positioned as the endgame destination for Diablo 4 once the credits roll.

Lord of Hatred, of course, as previously revealed, introduces two newly introduced endgame modes in War Prepares, and Echoing Hatred.

War Intends lets you create a custom playlist of up to five endgame activities to target specific rewards and create your own experience. There’s a fresh activity tree that works with all endgame activities, and creating War Plans is how you earn progression there.

Echoing Hatred, on the other hand, is a rare event that pits you against legions of Mephisto’s minions. It’s triggered through a rare lootable item that unlocks access. It’s essentially horde mode; where you’ll face unending waves of enemies, though not without a couple of twists.

Industry observers note that we also got a bit more colour on the expanded class skill trees, which all players will benefit from when the expansion arrives. The Talisman system, which unlocks set bonuses, was also shown off. And, of course, the return of the iconic Horadric Cube, which gives you control over Affixes.

The Anniversary Spotlight should’ve had a Year of the Warlock subtitle, because the class is also making its way to both Diablo Immortal, as well as Diablo 2: Resurrected. The showcase revealed the Reign of the Warlock DLC, which adds the aforementioned Warlock to D2R - its first new class in 25 years.

Sources indicate that reign of the Warlock, which is available now in D2R, also makes a few updates to the game, such as new quality of life features, the Colossal Ancients endgame encounter, updated Terror Zones and more. You also get some cosmetics in Diablo 4 if you purchase this expansion.

As we head towards the weekend, it's becoming increasingly cold and dark, and that means you'll probably want to sit and find a mobile game to sink plenty of time into. Well, you're in luck, because there's a constant glut of great new releases, including the launch of Dicevaders on iOS!

It has been revealed that dicevaders sees you taking on the role not of defender of the Earth, but of its invaders and destroyers. To do so, you'll need to gradually overwhelm the defences of each of Earth's bastions, and you'll do so with dice (naturally). In essence, you place units, build up multipliers and gradually overcome the defence rating of each planet to destroy it.

It makes for a rather interesting combination of luck and strategy, where you'll need to think about when you might need to reroll and keep your supply of currencies stocked up to do so. The graphics are, of course, the kind of crunchy, colourful pixels I'm fond of, so you won't hear any complaints from me, and the mix of blues, purples and reds makes for a thoroughly alien colour palette.

Industry observers note that there's plenty of synergy, different commanders and units to take advantage of too. So if you're looking for a game with plenty of depth to enjoy this winter, why not check out Dicevaders on iOS?

#156447. One type of physical activity is linked to a 20% higher dementia risk

General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

One type of physical activity is linked to a 20% higher dementia risk

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1305 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Regular physical activity has long been recognized as a way to help protect against dementia.
  • An analysis involving more than 4.2 million people found that recreational activities such as walking, cycling, running, swimming, and playing sports were associated with a significantly lower risk of dementia.
  • In a recent development, published in The Lancet Public Health, the study is the first systematic investigation into whether a phenomenon known as the "physical activity paradox" also applies to dementia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Regular physical activity has long been recognized as a way to help protect against dementia. However, latest research from the University of Southern California (USC) suggests that the circumstances in which people are physically active may be just as important as the amount of activity they get.

An analysis involving more than 4.2 million people found that recreational activities such as walking, cycling, running, swimming, and playing sports were associated with a significantly lower risk of dementia. Surprisingly, people who engaged in higher levels of physical activity at work appeared to face an increased risk of developing the condition.

In a recent development, published in The Lancet Public Health, the study is the first systematic investigation into whether a phenomenon known as the "physical activity paradox" also applies to dementia. Already well established in cardiovascular research, this paradox refers to the observation that physical labor does not necessarily offer the same health advantages as recreational exercise and may even be associated with a greater risk of disease.

According to recent reports, led by David Raichlen, professor of biological sciences and anthropology at the USC Dornsife College of Letters, Arts and Sciences, the research team examined data from 74 cohort and case-control studies. Together, the studies included more than 4.2 million people between the ages of 45 and 93 from 30 countries. Over a median follow-up period of 10 years, researchers monitored diagnoses of all-cause dementia, Alzheimer's disease, and vascular dementia.

Participants who engaged in higher levels of recreational physical activity had a 24% lower risk of dementia compared with the least active individuals. Physical activity associated with household chores also appeared to offer benefits, although this finding was supported by only one study. In contrast, higher levels of physical activity at work were linked to a 20% greater risk of dementia. Physically active commuting was also associated with a modest increase in risk, but evidence for this relationship came from just two studies.

"The findings challenge the long-held assumption that 'every move counts' for brain health," said Natan Feter, the study's first author, a postdoctoral fellow in Raichlen's Evolutionary Biology of Physical Activity Lab at USC and a researcher in the Graduate Program of Epidemiology at Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul (Brazil).

Why Exercise and Physical Labor May Affect the Brain Differently.

Researchers often group recreational exercise, manual labor, household chores, and active commuting together when measuring "Physical activity." However, the authors suggest that the circumstances surrounding these activities vary considerably and could influence their long-term health effects.

People who exercise during their free time generally have greater control over the intensity and nature of their activities. Recreational exercise can also provide opportunities to socialize and relieve stress. In comparison, physically demanding occupations may require repeated movements, extended periods of standing, heavy lifting, and insufficient time to recover, along with exposure to potentially harmful workplace conditions.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers do not believe that physical movement itself is likely to explain the elevated dementia risk associated with occupational activity. Instead, the relationship may arise from the social and environmental factors commonly associated with manual labor.

It has been revealed that physically demanding occupations are more likely to expose workers to psychological and social stress, limited control over their work, unsafe conditions, and higher levels of air and noise pollution. Each of these factors has independently been associated with dementia risk. Workers may also struggle to participate in recreational exercise because of exhaustion, limited free time, or a lack of access to safe spaces for physical activity.

Opposing Patterns in Dementia Risk.

The researchers also discovered that the relationship between physical activity and dementia risk was not linear and followed opposite patterns depending on the type of activity.

Industry observers note that as recreational exercise increased, dementia risk gradually declined until the apparent benefits leveled off. Occupational physical activity showed the reverse pattern, with dementia risk increasing at higher activity levels before eventually reaching a plateau.

Key Limitations and Unanswered Questions.

The authors emphasize that there is still too little research on physical activity related to household chores and commuting to draw definitive conclusions about either. Most of the available evidence also comes from high-income countries, despite projections that low- and middle-income nations will experience the greatest increases in dementia cases in the coming decades.

According to recent reports, another limitation is that almost all the studies depended on participants reporting their own physical activity. This approach can introduce errors if people do not accurately remember their activity levels. Nevertheless, Feter mentioned the consistency of the findings across several additional statistical analyses suggests that the observed relationships warrant serious attention.

According to recent reports, the researchers stress that their findings should not discourage people from pursuing physically active occupations. Since the analysis relied on observational research, it cannot establish that occupational physical activity causes dementia.

Instead, the results underscore the importance of examining the conditions under which people are physically active. Recreational exercise continued to be associated with a lower risk of dementia, while occupational activity remained linked to a higher risk even after researchers accounted for differences in age, education, and chronic health conditions.

How Sedentary Activities May Also Influence Brain Health.

The importance of context may extend beyond physical activity. Separate research by Raichlen, Feter, and their colleagues, published recently in the journal Alzheimer's & Dementia, suggests that different types of sedentary behavior may also be associated with differences in brain structure.

In that study, mentally stimulating activities performed while sitting, such as working at a desk, were associated with greater volume in certain regions of the cerebral cortex than more passive activities, such as watching television. These differences included brain regions involved in executive function.

Together, the findings could have key implications for public health strategies aimed at reducing dementia risk. The authors suggest that encouraging people to "move more" may not be sufficient without also addressing the circumstances in which physical activity takes place.

"In other words, when it comes to protecting the brain, the context of physical activity may matter just as much as movement itself," Raichlen remarked. "Improving access to safe parks, walking trails and recreational facilities, ensuring people have adequate leisure time for exercise, and reducing harmful workplace exposures may ultimately prove as important as promoting physical activity itself.".

It has been revealed that raichlen and Feter's co-authors include Tiladia Markarian, Dylan M. Luong, Jack Gunnink, Anamika Nanda, Sarah Hourihan and Ashley Ventura of USC; Eduardo Caputo, Jayne Feter, Gustavo S. Silva and Airton José Rombaldi of Universidade Federal de Pelotas (Brazil); Paula Iso-Markku of the University of Helsinki (Finland); Daniela Benzano Bumaguin of Fundação Universitária de Cardiologia (Brazil); Yann C. Klimentidis and Gene E. Alexander of the University of Arizona; Daniel Umpierre and Natália Schröder of Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul (Brazil); and Pedro C. Hallal of University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign.

In a recent development, funding for the research included National Institutes of Health grants P30AG072980, P30AG019610, R56AG067200, R01AG064587 and R01AG072445, along with support from the state of Arizona, the Arizona Department of Health Services and the McKnight Brain Research Foundation. Additional financial support was provided in part by the Fundação de Amparo à Pesquisa do Estado do Rio Grande do Sul (FAPERGS) (25/2551-0002834-5) and the National Council for Scientific and Technological Development - CNPq and Department of Science and Technology of Secretariat of Science, Technology, Innovation and Health Complex of Ministry of Health of Brazil - MoH (445538/2023-6).

💡 Key Takeaways
  • GTA 6 is a technical marvel, one that's left a veteran game artist with credits on The Last of Us Part 2 Remastered and Star Wars Jedi: Survivor so stunned, he says he "didn't know this was possible.".
  • Del Walker is a lead character artist at Absurd Ventures who previously worked at Naughty Dog and Respawn Entertainment, and he's been giving his overwhelmingly positive thoughts on GTA 6 to Bloomberg reporter Jason Schreier (below).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GTA 6 is a technical marvel, one that's left a veteran game artist with credits on The Last of Us Part 2 Remastered and Star Wars Jedi: Survivor so stunned, he says he "didn't know this was possible.".

Del Walker is a lead character artist at Absurd Ventures who previously worked at Naughty Dog and Respawn Entertainment, and he's been giving his overwhelmingly positive thoughts on GTA 6 to Bloomberg reporter Jason Schreier (below). Referring specifically to the game's graphics, he notes: "Everything they're doing is what we have been told never to do in every game I've been on.".

For example, Schreier explains that during his conversation with the dev, Walker pointed to the fact that you normally only see a few characters on screen at any point with realistic hair that actually moves strand by strand, with NPCs usually made in a modular way that makes them look generic. This sort of thing comes in an effort to achieve reasonable scope and 60fps, Schreier notes.

Obviously, though, not only did Rockstar opt for a 30fps target on PS5 and Xbox Series X|S, but the devs went above and beyond with the detail of their NPCs, with them being individually art directed and given their own personality traits to boot. As Walker puts it, "It's like looking at a skyscraper, but I'm from the 1800s. I didn't know this was possible.".

Recent findings suggest that he's not the only one impressed, of course. One game designer on The Last of Us Part 2 has called GTA 6 "the Great Pyramids of Game Development," saying that "people will be asking for centuries how it was possible and we will eventually conclude that aliens made it.".

It's for good reason, of course. Even with such a lengthy development cycle and a clearly immense budget (that Rockstar won't confirm beyond saying it's not $1.5 billion), GTA 6 really is a sight to behold – there's no wonder that other devs are contemplating the sorcery behind it. As Walker so eloquently puts it, "I don't know shit about fuck. Rockstar do, clearly.".

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, the class action suit was filed at the United States District Court for the Northern District of California in June this year.
  • In a recent development, the trio of companies deny having colluded, arguing in a newly introduced motion to have the case dismissed (thanks, IGN) that this suit simply retreads old ground covered in a previous antitrust case and quoting deceased judge Richard Posner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A judge has denied a motion to dismiss a US lawsuit against chip makers Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron. The suit acccuses the companies of fixing RAM prices and supply, thereby contributing to worsening the effects of the ongoing memory crisis.

In a recent development, the class action suit was filed at the United States District Court for the Northern District of California in June this year. It accuses Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron of moving in lockstep away from production of consumer-focused DDR3 and DDR4 RAM and towards HBM memory more typically used in AI datacenters. The suit claims that "in a competitive commodity market", "at least one of three large producers, seeing record prices, would expand output of the product whose price was rising", thereby forcing their competitors to either follow suit or risk losing out on customers.

In a recent development, the trio of companies deny having colluded, arguing in a newly introduced motion to have the case dismissed (thanks, IGN) that this suit simply retreads old ground covered in a previous antitrust case and quoting deceased judge Richard Posner. "[C]ompetitors in concentrated markets watch each other like hawks," was the Posner quote they wheeled out, which I mention because otherwise the response I'm about to lay out will sound like a very weird tangent.

In a recent development, "But Plaintiffs’ allegations go beyond hawks watching each other," judge Noël Wise wrote in her order to deny the dismissal motion. "Their contentions are more akin to hawks flying in formation – an activity that hawks ordinarily do not do.".

Sources indicate that you know a case is getting serious when facts about Avian behaviour start being wheeled out in response to similes. Bird chatter aside, all this decision means is that the case will rumble on, with both sides still having a chance to present more evidence or make points in their favour before any eventual decision is made by the courts.

So, shelve any hopes you might have of a rapid solution to the memory crisis, which currently looks likely to last until at least 2028.

#156441. 10 Elements Metroidvanias Could Borrow From GTA 6

10 Elements Metroidvanias Could Borrow From GTA 6

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1613 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dualshockers

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As someone who usually writes about Metroidvanias but has recently been engrossed in GTA 6, I haven't stopped thinking about the points where the two converge.
  • Rockstar's latest work isn't an adventure like the series' previous iterations; instead, it boasts an even finer and more meticulous design that, at fleeting moments, makes me feel it hides lessons beyond the obvious.
  • That games in its genre will follow in its footsteps is logical, but I truly believe there's a sufficiently diverse level of excellence to consider that not only open-world titles will benefit from its influence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As someone who usually writes about Metroidvanias but has recently been engrossed in GTA 6, I haven't stopped thinking about the points where the two converge.

Rockstar's latest work isn't an adventure like the series' previous iterations; instead, it boasts an even finer and more meticulous design that, at fleeting moments, makes me feel it hides lessons beyond the obvious.

That games in its genre will follow in its footsteps is logical, but I truly believe there's a sufficiently diverse level of excellence to consider that not only open-world titles will benefit from its influence.

Therefore, in order to return to writing about the type of games I'm passionate about while still fulfilling my communicative responsibility towards the interactive entertainment industry's latest titan, here are ten elements Metroidvanias could borrow from GTA 6.

Throughout its history, Grand Theft Auto has been a franchise of journeys, stories, and mechanics that unfold along the way rather than at the destination, giving vehicles a prominent role as in GTA 6.

In contrast, movement in Metroidvanias, despite the notable importance of exploration, is reduced to the characters and their abilities, limiting the worlds' scale to the equally slow speed at which their protagonists move.

Therefore, as the final stages of each campaign approach, fast travel becomes the key to backtracking, so the presence of manually controllable means of transport would not only add another layer of depth but also enable even larger worlds.

It doesn't have to be permanent, of course, as I personally love concrete maps that you can traverse on foot, yet the genre would benefit from a broader understanding of distance than it has been done so far.

Although I don't believe every game should have a plethora of minigames and side activities like GTA 6, I do think they highlight the narrow imagination with which Metroidvanias approach their gameplay concepts.

Speaking of verbs, fighting and moving are the only ones that can be attributed to their vast majority, instead of including more interactive elements that would help diversify the gaming experience.

Silver Pines, for example, does an excellent job in this regard by inheriting puzzles from horror games, but visual novels' decision-making, RPGs' morality systems, or stealth games' infiltrative sections could have a place in the right products.

Of course, it's easier to have diverse gameplay if you're an open-world game than if you're an action-adventure title, since the classification limits you, though I think it's a good time to break free from the shackles of labels.

Especially since FromSoftware's games have influenced the genre, it's become increasingly difficult to find a Metroidvania with a concrete story, told linearly and directly rather than through contextual and ambiguous elements.

These are rich and fertile narrative mechanisms for creating immersive worlds, no doubt, but the trope easily becomes exhausted after practically everyone resorts to it to tell their tales.

I'm not necessarily talking about cinematics or actors with impressive performances, but about campaigns with concrete beginnings, developments, and endings, as Prince of Persia: The Lost Crown and Ori and the Blind Forest have already done.

These examples demonstrate that it's achievable, and if we dare to go further and adopt a love story as emotional and sensitive as Jason and Lucia's, all the better.

Returning to the premise of gameplay variety, Metroidvanias have failed to convey the influence of their environments beyond the visual, as our ways of interacting with different biomes remain virtually unchanged.

You don't usually dive into aquatic biomes, just as you don't climb mountainous areas or sink into swamps, because the way we orient ourselves in space tends to be the same regardless of that location's unique characteristics.

In contrast, GTA 6 does a superb job of differentiating each of its regions, with activities adapted to the physical attributes of each one to truly convey the feeling that the world you're inhabiting exists.

I'm not suggesting the same level of depth or technological detail, but rather the same approach: to turn aesthetic beauty into playable immersion.

GTA 6, with its massive wardrobe and extensive customization system, reminded me of how special it felt to see Alucard's simple cape color change in Castlevania: Symphony of the Night depending on his equipment.

When you think of the greatest Metroidvanias, we all know and play the same protagonist, from their visual presentation to their gameplay styles, as the options are kept to a minimum to ensure precision and refinement.

It's a perfectly valid design sacrifice, and it has given us countless masterpieces, yet invalidating player expression by not allowing them to create their own unique gameplay and aesthetic combinations is a debt that has gone unpaid for years.

It's easier said than done, considering how much more difficult it is to conceive of an avatar that offers so many alternatives, but it's so captivating in GTA 6 that I can't help but dream with the possibility.

Even with the perpetual satire and exaggeration inherent in GTA 6's story, it reminded me how unusual realistic narratives have become within the video game industry, which is at the mercy of various forms of fantasy instead.

Thus, would playing a Metroidvania governed by our universal laws be even remotely as entertaining as one with an entirely newly introduced world? I don't have the slightest idea, precisely because this approach is so unexplored within the genre.

The conversations between Jason and Lucia feel so human, as do many of the events with NPCs and secondary characters, that you empathize almost instinctively, leading to a level of connection unusual in Metroidvanias.

Works like Shadow Complex or, to a lesser extent, Silver Pines itself, partially demonstrate this possibility, and I feel that exploring it would help open up a completely unique avenue for the genre, one that isn't limited to hand-drawn 2D side-scrollers.

Sources indicate that among the most striking aspects of GTA 6 is the way every NPC reacts to your every move. Whether it's walking, wearing unusual clothing, drawing a weapon, or saying something, there's an interaction waiting for you around every corner.

In the context of Metroidvanias, games like Hollow Knight have already explored the idea of characters responding to our actions, and even with the system's restrictions, it's an integral element of its worldbuilding.

Accordingly, building on that foundation and with an eye on Leonida's organic world, campaigns can be created where we feel our influence isn't rigidly predetermined but rather gradually constructed on both a macro and micro level.

It's difficult to anticipate the rapid arrival of a structure with such ramifications due to the predominance of independent developers in the genre, though simply having the horizon in sight is enough to begin moving towards it.

Ever since I played The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim, I've realized that progression in video games is almost always extradiegetic—that is, it happens before the player's eyes, not so much the character's—and GTA 6 also rejected this principle.

Consequently, "finding" a skill instead of developing it is a statement in itself about how a character grows, which is quite functional for the Metroidvania philosophy but not so much for the feeling of evolving through our gameplay experience.

I doubt it's interesting to lock the double jump behind having to go to the gym and do jumping jacks for a whole week, yet a game where our combat and movement skills expand based on how we interact with its base mechanics is a future that excites me.

GTA 6 makes it very simple, and sometimes it's even annoying, but the fact that it works here for the sake of realism doesn't mean that Metroidvanias can't use the same methodology for the sake of fun.

In Metroidvanias, there's no such thing as approaches: you either play the way the game wants you to, or you simply have to give up on the possibility of finishing it altogether.

GTA 6, inevitably, is also a slave to determinism, yet it leans slightly towards immersive sim design, allowing you to choose how you're going to fulfill your unchangeable obligations.

There are fights you can avoid with dialogue, wars you can replace with stealthy takedowns, and conflicts you can relocate with distraction tactics, thanks in part to a level design that offers more than one way to handle its execution.

I would never ask a Metroidvania to be Dishonored, though I could respectfully request that it at least try to integrate the possibility that not every challenge is solved by depleting a boss's health bar or completing an artificial platforming challenge.

I'd be lying if I didn't say I'm quite a fan of the true ending trope hidden behind an obscure side mission that unfolds outside the main campaign, but it does sadden me that it's the only option Metroidvanias often display.

While GTA 6 emphasizes numerous decisions, circumstances, and systems that occur at pivotal points in the plot and throughout the game, Metroidvanias have a much more reductive model.

Regardless of how you play, games in this genre tend to follow the formula of "good ending, bad ending by changing a decision before the final boss, true ending behind an optional mission", and it's starting to lose its appeal.

Certainly, GTA 6's approach isn't necessarily revolutionary or life-changing, yet it's complex enough to make you think about how you interact with its systems, so it more than achieves its goal.

Of course, for there to be impactful decisions to make, it's necessary to apply several of the fundamentals mentioned in this list, as they can't be achieved in isolation. However, since Rockstar's game will surely be the benchmark for many years to come, I'm sure some lessons will sink in.

#156439. A tiny injectable sensor could change how millions of people monitor blood sugar

A tiny injectable sensor could change how millions of people monitor blood sugar

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (865 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Continuous glucose monitors help millions of people with diabetes keep track of their glucose levels in real time, making it easier to manage medications, dietary choices, and everyday activities.
  • Scientists at Texas A&M University have identified a potential way to make future glucose monitors more affordable.
  • Many existing glucose monitoring technologies depend on enzymes to detect glucose.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Continuous glucose monitors help millions of people with diabetes keep track of their glucose levels in real time, making it easier to manage medications, dietary choices, and everyday activities. However, the high cost of these devices prevents some patients from accessing the technology.

Scientists at Texas A&M University have identified a potential way to make future glucose monitors more affordable. In a study published in ACS Measurement Science AU, the researchers found that a key sensing material for an experimental injectable glucose sensor performed just as well as a commonly used alternative at approximately one-tenth of the cost.

Many existing glucose monitoring technologies depend on enzymes to detect glucose. The Texas A&M team is pursuing a different approach that uses fluorescent molecules and near-infrared light. By measuring variations in the fluorescent signal, researchers can determine changes in glucose concentration without relying on enzymes.

Sources indicate that the technology relies on a process called competitive binding. Within the sensor, glucose and a fluorescent sugar compound compete to occupy binding sites on a protein called concanavalin A, or ConA. As glucose levels rise, this competition alters the fluorescent signal, providing a way to measure glucose concentration.

Sources indicate that after evaluating several compounds that bind to the protein, the team identified β-mannopentaose as a promising alternative to α-mannopentaose, a more expensive compound used in previous versions of the sensor. Despite its substantially lower price, β-mannopentaose delivered comparable sensing performance. It also produced promising results in artificial interstitial fluid, a laboratory solution that recreates conditions beneath the skin.

Cutting Glucose Sensor Costs by 90%.

"The surprising part was how closely the lower-cost material matched the performance of the more expensive alternative," remarked Dr. Sayantan Tripathy, assistant research scientist in Texas A&M's Optical and Bio-Sensing Laboratory and the study's lead author. "In this case, the cheaper option wasn't really a compromise, and that's an important finding when you're thinking about future glucose-monitoring technologies.".

Sources indicate that "Developing an affordable glucose sensor means considering the cost of the individual materials as well as how well they work together," stated Dr. Gérard L. Coté, principal investigator of the study and a professor of biomedical engineering in the College of Engineering. "This study indicates that we can substantially reduce the cost of one sensing component while maintaining comparable performance, giving us a promising foundation for further development.".

A Tiny Injectable Sensor Beneath the Skin.

To create an injectable sensor, the researchers embedded the glucose detection materials within a small hydrogel designed to remain in the tissue beneath the skin. The gel holds the sensing materials in place while allowing glucose molecules to move through it, where their concentration can be measured.

Sources indicate that during laboratory experiments, more than 94% of the sensing assay remained within the hydrogel after seven days. The results demonstrate that the less expensive sensing chemistry is compatible with an injectable glucose monitoring system.

According to recent reports, "When upcoming medical technologies are expensive, access can be limited," remarked Dr. Melissa Grunlan, study co-author, professor of biomedical engineering in the College of Engineering and professor of chemistry in the College of Arts and Sciences. "Our goal is to develop sensors that are not only effective but affordable for the people who rely on them.".

Although the experimental sensor has shown encouraging results, it remains at the proof-of-concept stage. Further development and testing will be necessary before the technology can be considered for clinical use. Nevertheless, the findings indicate that reducing material costs does not necessarily require sacrificing sensing performance.

Making Diabetes Monitoring More Accessible.

The research highlights the importance of factoring affordability into the design of new medical technologies from the outset. Finding ways to reduce manufacturing expenses while maintaining performance could eventually expand access to continuous glucose monitoring, particularly among patients who cannot right now afford advanced monitoring devices.

The researchers intend to further refine their technology and investigate other components that could enhance its performance, extend its useful lifespan, and make it more practical.

"While the work remains in the research stage, the findings suggest that future glucose-monitoring technologies may not have to rely on expensive materials to deliver effective results," Tripathy mentioned.

According to recent reports, "Our long-term goal is to develop a reliable, affordable injectable glucose sensor that can expand access to continuous glucose monitoring, particularly for people in under-resourced communities and those without adequate insurance coverage," Coté remarked. "Reducing the cost of the sensing materials is one step toward making these technologies accessible to more people who need them.".

It has been revealed that the research team consisted entirely of Texas A&M researchers. Alongside Tripathy, Coté, and Grunlan, the team included Dr. Carolina Martinez, Anthony Dongchau, and Samyucktha Ganesapandian. Funding was provided by the National Science Foundation (NSF) Engineering Research Center for Precise Advanced Technologies and Health Systems for Under-resourced Populations.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Split-screen multiplayer is often treated by developers as a forgotten vestige of a bygone age, something to be left behind as the standardisation of online play makes it redundant, especially following the pandemic.
  • This latest mode, Free Play, not only allows for local multiplayer of up to four players (with either humans or CPUs racing together), but also for complete freedom of choice in vehicle, character and planet to race on.
  • Recent findings suggest that as for why this feature may not have been available at launch, other than the cynical view that it wasn't considered a moneymaking priority for Fuse Games and Secret Mode, CD Projekt Red senior technical producer Shayna Moon weighed in to theorise that it took some effort to get four separately-rendered views of the game running without making their machine explode like the Death Star.

Split-screen multiplayer is often treated by developers as a forgotten vestige of a bygone age, something to be left behind as the standardisation of online play makes it redundant, especially following the pandemic. It's considered unlikely that you'll have another human being in your home to pick up a controller with you, and since you've inevitably got an internet connection, why not just use that to connect to anyone in the world? I find there's a unique beauty in playing something shoulder to shoulder on a couch with another person, and it seems Fuse Games sees that light too, with Star Wars: Galactic Racer set to be updated to add local splitscreen multiplayer sometime early next year.

This latest mode, Free Play, not only allows for local multiplayer of up to four players (with either humans or CPUs racing together), but also for complete freedom of choice in vehicle, character and planet to race on. A simple versus mode like this is a far cry from the roguelite structure of the main game, and one that draws it closer to its arcade racing game roots. An embracing of that is always welcome, as Galactic Racer has been a reminder to many of just how wonderful the arcade racing genre can be, and how poorly served its been in the industry for a while. For example, while the Fuse Games team is partly made up of Criterion Games veterans, Criterion itself has recently been folded into being a Battlefield Studio by EA, making the future of Need for Speed and Burnout uncertain.

Recent findings suggest that as for why this feature may not have been available at launch, other than the cynical view that it wasn't considered a moneymaking priority for Fuse Games and Secret Mode, CD Projekt Red senior technical producer Shayna Moon weighed in to theorise that it took some effort to get four separately-rendered views of the game running without making their machine explode like the Death Star. As Moon puts it: "To be overly simple about it, if the game is running at 30fps for each player, that means it’s actually rendering 120fps." Likely not an concern for a lot of PC players, but a potential issue for console players considering the game is built to run at a locked 60fps for one player on consoles. Past this upcoming revision, it looks like the Star Wars franchise as a whole could be set for more smaller games ala Galactic Racer in general, per comments made by Lucasfilms' vice president.

You play as a slime with three sticky limbs, and have to alternate between them as you travel across levels, dodging obstacles and seeking out your gold coin as you go.

It has been revealed that and that, I reckon, is why we like covering Tepes' stuff. It's a throwback to the days of mobile when a solid, original concept done well could become the new darling of the app store. Even if now, for better or worse, we have so much more variety.

GTA 6 has notably launched without a PC release, landing on PlayStation 5 and the Xbox Series X|S only – a debacle that has, of course, led to fans attempting to get the Grand Theft Auto entry running on computers.

There are various "projects," so to speak, attempting to tackle an unofficial PC port – but one in particular made rounds recently after Rockstar allegedly took its Discord server down and prompted its lead – an anonymous 15-year-old (as per their own words) – to say "goodbye," noting that "managing school and sports is hard enough without having middle-aged men yell and complain to you on Discord." Well, they're back… and so is their project, Leonida. And, according to a newly introduced post on Twitter from "NotRexed," the Leonida lead, they'll provide more information on their supposed GTA 6 PC port in the coming days. "Leonida is NOT dead," they write. "I have been doing a lot of work behind the scenes. I'll have some stuff to show all of you soon." They follow up on this with a response stating that Leonida should feature "native Linux support," with "more on that later.".

Recent findings suggest that obviously, it's difficult to verify anything they say, seeing as this is a (very) unofficial port, should it be happening at all. Rockstar itself hasn't actually spoken on the matter publicly. It all stemmed from notorious GTA 6 leaker "Cyberleek," who recently uploaded an executable file and the Xbox build of the game online. Shortly after, fans like NotRexed picked it up and began working toward a PC version of Grand Theft Auto 6.

I'm not so sure what'll happen from here, but I am personally left wondering when Rockstar will announce an official PC release of the game. It's no small launch, after all, smashing records as the highest-rated game of all time on Metacritic and proving "the biggest launch in PlayStation history" (with Sony reporting "more than 39 million unique players" playing on the PS5 alone). Imagine how those numbers could grow….

Sources indicate that nioh 3 has received a hot new update that brings plenty of bug fixes to very specific issues, but it also implements fixes for a few of the most common - and incredibly annoying - bugs. Patch 1.03.01 arrived earlier on all platforms, and it comes with a chunky set of notes.

This latest update, predictably, doesn’t add any gameplay features, but some of the included fixes will absolutely delight - or vindicate - so many of the game’s millions of players.

There’s plenty to go through in the patch notes published today for update 1.03.01, but the most impactful is a fix for an issue that “sometimes made it impossible to use elixirs during battle.” This is only a partial fix, but if you ran into the problem of smashing that shortcut button and not seeing your character play the healing animation, you’ll be glad to see it.

It has been revealed that this is a problem myself and others have faced, especially in boss fights. You can even see the shortcut register your button press and proceed to ignore you. Another partial fix has been made to an concern that caused the game to crash. Team Ninja didn’t share specifics on that, and though Nioh 3 has been fairly stable for me in 70+ hours, it has definitely crashed a few times.

If you’ve been playing since launch, you likely have - or know someone who has - run into concerns with save file corruption and other weird bugs around certain trackable items within save files.

Team Ninja already rolled out a couple of fixes there, and this latest one specifically targets losing valuables during Myths. If your save file has been affected, the game will now check and recover what was lost. Even more interesting is that the game will now automatically create a backup copy of your save data any time you load a save.

If you’ve made it into the Eternal Rift, you’ll be happy to know that today’s update takes care of a few progression blockers, and fixes an matter that allowed some players to obtain certain items before they were supposed to, locking themselves out.

One of the more amusing fixes concerns Mujina, who had a tendency to respawn if you prayed at a Shrine after opening a chest it was hiding in, which made it appear far more often than a mimic should.

Industry observers note that finally, there’s a set of fixes that address bugs (and exploits) when using specific Martial Art with certain weapons. There are a few fixes to AI, Myths, and one problem with the Minamoto no Yoritomo boss fight that made it impossible to interrupt him, even after he runs out of Ki.

Recent findings suggest that hit the link at the top for the full change log, and check out our Nioh 3 gameplay tips if you haven’t already. You should also change these settings ASAP, as they’re going to make your life much easier and save you a lot of time.

Shopify Rebellion Black opened the North America Qualifier Playoffs with a 2-0 win over Xora Esports. The non-partner organisation is now one win from the playoffs that decide a guaranteed São Paulo Kickoff place.

The best-of-three Group Stage meeting with Xora began at 00:10 UTC on Saturday 21 November, opening Shopify Rebellion Black’s VCT Americas Kickoff: North America 2027 campaign.

The result counts for more because Shopify Rebellion is now outside Riot’s partnership system. The organisation was one of the Americas sides that mentioned it had not been chosen for the 2027-2028 partnership programme, Sheep Esports reported. Cloud9, ENVY, M80, FlyQuest and LYON were also on that list. Riot now has eight partner teams in each of its four regions.

The Swiss Stage runs from 20 to 22 November 2026. Every match is best of three. Two wins send a team through to the playoffs, and two losses knock it out. The eight teams left after the Swiss phase move into a double-elimination bracket played over six competition days, with the playoffs set for 1 to 6 December. The event is listed as an online, A-Tier Riot Games qualifier for 16 teams.

Recent findings suggest that shopify Rebellion Black’s next opponents are Oafs, who also won their opening match 2-0, against QoR. Both teams are therefore one win from the playoffs. Oafs already have a record against Xora. They knocked them out of the Qualifier 1 bracket on 8 November with a 2-1 win. Xora had still reached the Qualifier Playoffs by finishing joint third in the 512-team North America Qualifier 1.

Recent findings suggest that across 83 rated matches, Shopify Rebellion Black hold a 59-24 record. Before this event their most recent series was a 2-3 defeat to 2GAME Esports at the VCL Americas Last Chance Qualifier 2026. Earlier in that event they had beaten 2GAME Esports 2-1 and Contra 2-0.

The organisation’s second line-up had a harder start. Shopify Rebellion Gold lost 0-2 to Maryville University. Several of the other organisations left out of the partnership programme won their first matches. Cloud9 beat counterfeit 2-0, Team Envy beat Yellow Dragon Gaming 2-0 and FlyQuest edged Masterclass 2-1. Elsewhere, Winthrop University beat SaD Esports 2-0 and YFP Gaming beat Wildcard 2-1.

According to recent reports, the prize for coming through the bracket is a place in São Paulo. Riot will stage the 2027 VCT Americas Kickoff in Brazil. Its eight Partner Teams get direct entry. Non-partner teams can win four places: one guaranteed slot each for North America, Brazil and Latin America, plus one for the Americas Last Chance Qualifier. For a non-partner side, a later run to Masters would be worth a fixed US$200,000 and a place at Champions US$400,000, Dot Esports reported. The regional Kickoff events are due to start on 14 January 2027 and run until 7 February 2027.

#156432. Tech Report: Break up and re-commodify a fallen Earth in Steel Gullet, a satisfyingly funereal factory puzzler that really loves thermodynamics

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (647 w)
📖 Baca

Tech Report: Break up and re-commodify a fallen Earth in Steel Gullet, a satisfyingly funereal factory puzzler that really loves thermodynamics

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (647 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It's amazing what a difference a few lines of preamble can make to your understanding of a game.
  • The difference is that you're doing this inside a huge walking fortress city, which stamps across the surface of a largely unseen, devastated and uninhabitable Earth.
  • From a certain, carefully limited point of view, this transforms Steel Gullet into the kind of "Zen experience" I hope death-positive morticians have when really absorbed in their work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's amazing what a difference a few lines of preamble can make to your understanding of a game. Out now on PC, Steel Gullet is a factory engineering puzzler that, while notable for its meticulous interest in thermodynamics, broadly compares to the foundational work of Zachtronics, together with more recent and focussed conveyor belt wranglers such as Modulus. Resources come in, and you arrange machines on a grid to transform them into something else, before sliding them into an output hopper.

The difference is that you're doing this inside a huge walking fortress city, which stamps across the surface of a largely unseen, devastated and uninhabitable Earth. Your resources are the refuse of a bygone human civilisation: knots of concrete and rebar, flaccid rubber hose and splintered plank, that must be separated out before you can manufacture anything.

From a certain, carefully limited point of view, this transforms Steel Gullet into the kind of "Zen experience" I hope death-positive morticians have when really absorbed in their work. My task is to lay a civilisation to rest, by dissecting and cleansing the remains, readying a fallen objectworld for an after-life that extends somewhere beyond the map's huge rusty walls (walls that, perhaps appropriately, constrain your camera movement a bit too much for comfort).

It makes me think of the vertigo I get when I look at devices such as, well, the computer I'm writing this on, and think about how many materials and histories of production lie entangled within it. Steel Gullet answers the desire for clarity and accounting there. Of course, the other part of the premise is that I am doing busywork for some kind of totalitarian organisation, G.R.I.D. But shh, no time to think about that! I'm trying to work out how hot rubber needs to be before it can be moulded.

Thermodynamics is Steel Gullet's fixation, and a worthwhile one. Every material encased in each lump of salvage has different physical properties – a melting point, density, solubility, ferromagnetism, etcetera. You meed to exploit these differences to separate the pieces. Wood, for example, is more buoyant than metal and concrete, so if you feed the clump into an oil bath, the planks will float to the top. If there's rubber, you can run the clump through furnaces to melt and drain it, then cool and reheat the resulting puddle to create a malleable material.

It's still just the usual automation game routine of funnelling greebly wotsits through various smashy boxes to produce a commodity. But the thermodynamics sim element both supports the above feeling of purifying a hopelessly muddled world, and makes for a surprising visual feast: I enjoy watching each material emerge from the inital jumble and assume different shapes. There are the usual supporting infrastructure elements, such as elevators, splitters and manual junction boxes. I dare say somebody will build a logic circuit in Steel Gullet, sooner or later - let's start the clock till they get Doom running on the thing.

In terms of overall strategy, you alternate between sending outputs to hoppers that earn you cash, and sending them to hoppers that generate research progression. You'll also unlock latest rooms, removing walls and exposing new output hoppers. As you're issued new work orders, you must break open your production lines to install new machines and redirect the flow. Fortunately, you can sell back components to keep your cash reserves healthy – or at least, you can in the demo.

Between chapters, you'll be invited to join the resistance against the aforesaid G.R.I.D., perhaps sending information to the rebels. But again, no time, no time! I have all this concrete I need to powderise, all these girders I need to liquefy and make new, all these crisp, gleaming circuitboards I need to manufacture. The city's hunger is as vast as it is holy. Read more on Steam.

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (923 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, oxygen is essential for human survival and for most forms of life.
  • In the brain, excessive oxygen levels have been linked to a rare and often fatal childhood disorder called 3-MGA, as well as Leigh syndrome (the most common pediatric mitochondrial disease), Parkinson's disease, and premature aging.
  • Industry observers note that for the past decade, Gladstone Investigator Isha Jain, PhD, has studied how oxygen levels influence health and disease.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, oxygen is essential for human survival and for most forms of life. Yet under certain conditions, it can become dangerously toxic, causing serious damage to the body.

In the brain, excessive oxygen levels have been linked to a rare and often fatal childhood disorder called 3-MGA, as well as Leigh syndrome (the most common pediatric mitochondrial disease), Parkinson's disease, and premature aging. Researchers at Gladstone Institutes are now investigating a promising approach that could potentially help treat these conditions by reducing the amount of oxygen available to the body, a strategy known as hypoxia therapy.

Industry observers note that for the past decade, Gladstone Investigator Isha Jain, PhD, has studied how oxygen levels influence health and disease. Her research has explored how the reduced oxygen availability at high altitudes can produce beneficial effects in conditions ranging from Leigh syndrome and diabetes to solid tumors.

Expanding the Potential of Hypoxia Therapy.

Jain and her colleagues wanted to determine whether lowering oxygen levels could also benefit people with other rare and common conditions involving mitochondrial dysfunction and neurological damage.

For a fresh study published in Nature Metabolism, the team partnered with James Shorter, PhD, professor of biochemistry and biophysics at the University of Pennsylvania, and Daniel Southworth, PhD, professor of biochemistry and biophysics at UC San Francisco.

The researchers discovered that a malfunctioning protein known as HTRA2 can cause oxygen to accumulate to dangerous levels in tissues. Remarkably, reducing the oxygen concentration in the air dramatically extended lifespan and improved brain function in mice experiencing motor neuron degeneration caused by defective HTRA2.

"This protein is linked to many other conditions, so our findings suggest that hypoxia therapy could be transformative for treating many neurological diseases," states Jain, who is also a core investigator at Arc Institute.

How Excess Oxygen Becomes Toxic to the Brain.

It has been revealed that most cells contain tiny structures called mitochondria, which use oxygen to generate the energy the body needs to function. One of the most important components of this energy production system is Complex 1, the largest molecular machine within the mitochondria's respiratory machinery.

"Every time we breathe, 90 percent of the oxygen we consume goes to our mitochondria," states Ankur Garg, PhD, postdoctoral fellow in Jain's lab and first author of the study. "But if Complex 1 malfunctions, the mitochondria can no longer burn off oxygen at normal rates.".

Industry observers note that when mitochondria lose their ability to consume oxygen efficiently, the unused oxygen can accumulate in surrounding tissues and eventually reach toxic levels. This process can contribute to the brain damage associated with certain mitochondrial and neurological disorders. The researchers suspected that reducing oxygen availability might help prevent some of this damage.

Identifying Genetic Causes of Oxygen Toxicity.

It has been revealed that to identify diseases that might respond to hypoxia therapy, the team revisited data from an earlier large experiment. They searched for genes whose absence impaired cell growth under normal oxygen conditions but allowed cells to grow normally when oxygen levels were reduced.

By comparing these results with a database of known genetic disorders, the researchers identified 75 genes directly associated with diseases that could potentially benefit from hypoxia therapy.

According to recent reports, among the most promising candidates was the gene encoding HTRA2. Further investigation revealed that HTRA2 works alongside another protein (CLPB) to maintain the structural integrity of Complex 1.

"Together, these two proteins act like a clean-up crew inside mitochondria, preventing the machinery from becoming clogged with clumps of misfolded proteins," says Jain.

According to recent reports, the team found that when HTRA2 and CLPB are absent or malfunctioning, this cellular maintenance system breaks down. As a result, a critical component of Complex 1 stops functioning properly.

Breathing Less Oxygen Triples Lifespan in Mice.

To determine whether reducing oxygen levels could provide therapeutic benefits in a living organism, the researchers conducted experiments on mice deficient in HTRA2.

Mice that breathed air containing less oxygen lived three times as long as those breathing normal atmospheric air, which contains approximately 21 percent oxygen. The treatment also reduced inflammation in the striatum, a region of the brain.

Industry observers note that "By showing these mice could be successfully treated with low oxygen, our study expands the potential of hypoxia therapy to a wide range of conditions that affect mitochondrial Complex 1, either directly or indirectly as in the case of HTRA2 deficiency," Garg says. "This will motivate a broader application of 'turning the oxygen dial' to conditions ranging from rare genetic diseases to common neurological conditions and beyond.".

Developing a Drug That Mimics Low Oxygen.

According to recent reports, although the experiments involved having mice breathe air with reduced oxygen concentrations, Jain and her colleagues are working toward a more practical approach. They are developing a drug called HypoxyStat that could potentially reproduce the therapeutic benefits of low oxygen through a pill or injection.

"Right now, no treatments are uniformly available for mitochondrial diseases, and hypoxia therapy offers the hope that we could treat not just one, but many of these genetic conditions," Jain notes. "We're working hard to make it a practical treatment for human patients in the clinic.".
