It seems like we’re getting one of these every few months, but the world of mobile action RPGs that look like the games that, just a few years back, were only possible on consoles is expanding with another latest entry.

Netmarble, a studio and publisher known for its free-to-play games on mobile and PC, recently unveiled the launch date for The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin, its next major release that’s very much coming for the Genshin Impact crowd.

The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin is an open-world action RPG based on the world of The Seven Deadly Sins anime and manga. The game takes place in the world of Britannia, which looks similar to the way it does in the anime.

In a recent development, that said, the story of the game is not based on the anime or manga, Instead, it’s an original story set in the universe of the show. You play as Prince Tristan of the Kingdom of Liones who must find a way to bring order back to Britannia.

The gameplay should be familiar to anyone who played a free-to-play action RPG in the last decade. It features action combat, a roster of diverse heroes that you assemble to form teams, and a large pretty world to explore where you’ll also get to meet new characters.

Speaking of which, while Origin has its own original story, expect to be teaming up with characters from the series - some of whom wouldn't be able to meet naturally. You can thank the game's multiversal story for that.

It has been revealed that beyond all the serious business of saving the world and battling monsters, The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin also has a cozy, relaxing side. You’ll be able to fish, cook, forage and take on the beauty of the world with your pals.

The game has a bit of an unusual release schedule. It’s set to arrive on PC, PS5, iOS, and Android. PC (Steam), and PS5 players will be able to jump in starting March 16, whereas the global mobile launch is scheduled for one week later, on March 23.

Sources indicate that you can pre-register right now on the official website if you’re interested in earning a few rewards when the game launches. You can, of course, always wishlist the game on Steam and the PlayStation Store, too.

#156405. The Most Loved and Hated JRPGs by Fans

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1634 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dualshockers ↗ Open Full Page

The Most Loved and Hated JRPGs by Fans

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1634 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dualshockers

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, JRPGs have long since become a distinct phenomenon as a specific subgenre of RPGs, even when they are not produced in Japan.
  • However, while there is a slightly more civilized consensus around what makes the best fighting game or racing game, the JRPGs fanbase always seems deeply divided.
  • I will alternate between hated and loved entries and avoid repeating franchises to keep the list dynamic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, JRPGs have long since become a distinct phenomenon as a specific subgenre of RPGs, even when they are not produced in Japan. Fixed characters, linear narratives, creative progression, and an atduesthetic usually inspired by anime are what tell us at a glance what makes a JRPG stand apart from any other subgenre under the role-playing umbrella. And to be honest, those exact elements are what draw me to the genre, sometimes removing one or adding another.

However, while there is a slightly more civilized consensus around what makes the best fighting game or racing game, the JRPGs fanbase always seems deeply divided. Some titles seem to sit at the same level of love and hate for fans, no matter which side you're on. That is why I decided to talk today about the most loved and most hated JRPGs by the public. This isn't a consensus or an objective truth, but a fun look at what I have observed after years on forums, debating with fellow JRPG lovers, and tracking the fanbase's overall perception.

I will alternate between hated and loved entries and avoid repeating franchises to keep the list dynamic.

According to recent reports, while I couldn't find a direct primary source confirming this claim, outlets like Kotaku and RPGFan say the same thing: due to Xenosaga Episode II flopping so hard, the series was cut from its intended six episodes to just three. For fans hoping to see Tetsuya Takahashi's vision fully realized, that was a massive blow and certainly left a mark of hatred on the second Xenosaga.

While Xenosaga Episode I: Der Wille zur Macht went over budget and featured far more cinematics than the average JRPG player was accustomed to (yeap), it was still a satisfactory experience. The second one? Not so much. The shift in art direction and the battle system genuinely pushed players away and, allegedly, led Bandai Namco to safeguard its investment by wrapping up the entire story as a trilogy. Much like Xenogears, Xenosaga became a beautiful what-could-have-been scenario, though luckily we eventually got to see Takahashi's ambitions realized with Xenoblade, which is still going strong.

To be completely honest, I am not that big of a fan of EarthBound. I played EarthBound Beginnings, also known as Mother, and found it impressive for an NES JRPG. Shortly after, I moved on to EarthBound, which I had played a long time ago and didn't remember much, and I walked away unimpressed. Maybe the American parody didn't resonate with me (I am not American), or maybe I played it too late, and the cultural zeitgeist didn't hit me the same way.

Recent findings suggest that even so, I fully recognize how much people who enjoy this JRPG truly adore it. They spare no praise, speak fondly of the experience, and admire not only the game itself, but also its creator, Shigesato Itoi. Many of those fans claim Mother 3, a title that never officially left Japan, is even better, but since I didn't vibe with the second entry, I have little interest in trying it.

It has been revealed that sometimes a game is hated for its themes, other times for an overly boring battle system, or perhaps because of an obnoxious character we cannot stand looking at. Occasionally, however, games draw hatred simply for feeling apathetic, failing to spark any real emotion in the player, and offering nothing particularly remarkable. That's exactly the case with Tales of Zestiria for many Tales fans.

According to recent reports, mind you, I actually enjoy the game, and it was the very first Tales of title where I earned the platinum trophy. I was never overly critical of Sorey's journey, the complex equipment fusion system, or even the misleading marketing around Alisha's protagonism. I mean, okay, fair enough, those all sound like completely valid points of criticism, yet I still had a good time. Not everyone can say the same, and whenever you look at a Tales of tier list, Zestiria almost always sits right at the bottom.

It has been revealed that apparently, there are two types of fans in the JRPG world: those who love Suikoden II and those who haven't played it yet. I am not kidding here. I considered adding Xenogears to this spot because I know it has a very vocal fanbase, quite scary to be honest, borderline toxic. But Suikoden? That feels like a genuine relationship, a true love situation. Every time you meet someone who notes Suikoden II is their favorite game, you can practically see their eyes light up.

To a large extent, I get it! Suikoden II is awesome. The grounded political plot stood out at a time when countless games were mostly about slaying God in a high fantasy setting. The 108 recruitable characters, each carrying their own motivation and reason for joining the resistance. The six-party-member battles with combo skills, and so on. Okay, you might need to use a walkthrough to recruit everyone and unlock the true ending, but the journey itself is already wonderful, and Luca Blight is a terrific villain. What is there not to love, right? Glory to Suikoden.

Industry observers note that there is nothing more miserable than watching a series you love, follow closely, and appreciate in every detail slowly fall from grace. For me, that didn't happen with Star Ocean, because I genuinely love Star Ocean: The Divine Force, though that is precisely how many felt after Star Ocean: Till the End of Time, the third entry. Plenty of fans didn't care for Star Ocean: The Last Hope yet could still stomach it, but Star Ocean: Integrity and Faithlessness? Just mentioning the name makes me feel your glare.

Recent findings suggest that the fifth Star Ocean suffered from an affliction that hit many JRPG franchises during that era: constricting budgets. I know that doesn't excuse its final quality, but it is the reality. The game severely lacked traditional cutscenes, playing out almost entirely through real-time in-engine camera angles, not out of artistic charm, but due to a lack of investment. I still like the game for two reasons: Item Creation remains incredible, and as someone who loves constantly swapping between party members, being able to deploy everyone into battle at once was a blast, even if having seven party members acting simultaneously got confusing and felt like a bit too much. It had a chaotic family reunion vibe, you know.

Out of all the JRPG fans I know, well over half say they discovered or fell in love with the genre after playing Final Fantasy VII. That fact alone could summarize this entire entry, because you either know someone just like that or you are that person yourself. I am a bit older, so I played other JRPGs before FFVII, though my cousin fits that exact mold, since he still uses an email address with the game's acronym in his handle to this day.

It is completely understandable, mind you. Final Fantasy VII was a global phenomenon that paved the way for JRPGs to gain worldwide recognition. That is why if you watch footage from the E3 showcase where the remake was unveiled, you will see countless explosive reactions. I know many newcomers to the genre or franchise don't understand why Square Enix split the remake into three parts, calling the firm mercenary (fitting for the game's plot, to be honest). Yet, I believe Square did it to honor the franchise's legacy, deliver something fresh for longtime fans, and naturally attract a new audience who can experience that same magic veterans felt when they first played and fell in love with it.

It has been revealed that whereas with most entries I listed as most hated (not hated by me, remember!) I tried to soften the blow and use euphemisms to avoid insulting people who enjoy those games or the developers behind them. For Lunar: Dragon Song, though, the gloves are completely off. I had only heard rumors about it, about how this mechanic was terrible and that feature was lousy, until one day I decided to test it for myself.

In a recent development, good lord, it is awful. So many baffling design decisions make me genuinely wonder how anyone let them pass. First, and most obviously, simply running in the game drains your HP. I mean, what? Then there are two separate reward modes per battle, one granting only experience points and another granting only loot. I didn't understand that system at first and left loot mode active, feeling bizarrely weak despite fighting endless battles. On top of that, combat has mandatory auto-targeting, plus a bland story, forgettable characters, and other uninspiring features. Lunar: Dragon Song is universally hated, and it deserves every bit of it.

Industry observers note that whenever someone asks me which JRPG I would recommend to a complete newcomer to the genre, the answer nine times out of ten is Chrono Trigger. Pointing to a 1995 release even today speaks volumes about the work's enduring relevance and timelessness. And I will go a step further: that recommendation doesn't rely on cheap nostalgia alone, because Chrono Trigger truly is a spectacle, with pacing, gameplay, and design that can captivate even the most stubborn skeptics who resist JRPGs.

Sources indicate that and of course, among JRPG enthusiasts, it is tough to find anyone who doesn't genuinely love Chrono Trigger. You might have critiques about it (I certainly do), or complain about one small detail or another. Still, it's nearly impossible to deny that it is a masterpiece and a majestic blueprint for building a JRPG. It stands undeniably as the most beloved JRPG of all time, even if you don't happen to be one of the people who love it.

Recent findings suggest that gloomwood, the Victorian survival horror immersive sim (or, wait, I'm getting reports that we shouldn't call it an immersive sim, apparently) by Dillon Rogers is a game that is quite happily inspired by its predecessors such as Thief, Resident Evil and Dishonored; you could call it 'Thief with guns', if you really wanted to. (Sorry, I've just seen that the domain for Gloomwood's site used to be 'residenthievil.com'. Wonderful). Now, that last inspiration has come full circle, as publisher Latest Blood Interactive's latest revision post confirms that the newest member of the team is none other than former Dishonored designer Julien Eveillé.

In a recent development, in addition to his work at Arkane on Dishonored and its sequel, Deathloop, and even Marvel's Blade, Eveillé also developed his own indie horror, 2024's short and sweet Threshold. It's quite a legacy to add to this team, and his hiring is described by Newly introduced Blood as an example of how "finding level designers who are up to the task of working on Gloomwood is not easy". The post also mentions that Eveillé will be added alongside "our new devs", implying that he's not the only new addition to the team.

It has been revealed that other than these fresh hires, the enhancement is set to include quite a bit to change up Gloomwood and make it bigger. The highlight is the First National Bank level, which is described as "our largest and most intricately designed level yet", with the screenshots showing off a grand and imposing, yet claustrophobic in places, that makes the act of going to the bank even more intimidating than usual. The Bank is joined by the new stun prod weapon, which is self-explanatory, and the new Rat and Fishdog transformations, which let you sneak through crawlspaces and swim through dirtied waters respectively. That sneaking will be made more difficult by the addition of alarms and blood pools that both alert surrounding guards to your presence, though the new Crow King transformation offers a new, acid-belching way to take down any guards that come running.

In a recent development, the enhancement is tentatively scheduled for "before the end of the year", but Newly introduced Blood aren't setting down a specific release date. Rogers himself will also be going through back surgery very soon, for which I wish him a gentle recovery and, hopefully, as easy a return to work as possible.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto VI is a game where you spend a lot of time behind the wheel. Always has been. But sometimes, you just won't feel like actively driving, but you also don't to waste money on a cab.

This is where Auto Drive comes in. It lets the game take over and drive you where you need to go in real time and all with a cinematic camera that shifts and moves, letting you take in the environment without all that pesky "having to pay attention to the road." Red Dead Redemption 2 had the same feature, and I have fond memories of taking advantage of it to watch Arthur ride his horse through that game's incredible environment. It's a great option in GTAVI, but how to use it and turn it on isn't immediately apparent.

Sources indicate that first, you must select a destination. Get the GPS set up to direct you to where you want to go.

It has been revealed that next, start driving. The Auto Drive is smart, but doesn't seem to be smart enough to make three-point turns or back out of parking lots. You need to be on your way before you can turn it on.

Once you're on the path, hold down in the d-pad and press start to activate Cinematic.

Recent findings suggest that once you've done this you should be able to hold down the Circle button on PlayStation or the B button on Xbox to activate Auto Drive and... voilà! You can sit back and let Jason or Lucia take the wheel. They will drive legally, even stopping at lights, but you can speed them up if they're taking too long.

I've always enjoyed driving in Grand Theft Auto, but I was grateful to find this almost-hidden option early in the game.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Things are officially looking better for Marathon. The game’s Server Slam, essentially an open beta that’s freely available everywhere, has kicked off. This is the last chance for anyone curious about Bungie’s next big game to play it before it officially goes on sale next week.

Considering how unpopular the game has been throughout its development, and judging by the feedback from earlier closed beta tests, the turnout for the Server Slam is definitely encouraging.

The Marathon Server Slam has been online for a little over 12 hours on Steam, PS5, and Xbox Series X/S. Only one of those platforms shares player numbers, of course, but it's enough to offer some visibility into how popular the test has been.

In a recent development, immediately after servers went live, Marathon shot up the Steam most played charts. The game swiftly achieved a peak of 143,621 concurrent players (via SteamDB), which is very respectable. Given that the Server Slam will be available for the entire weekend, there’s every chance the numbers will go up.

In a recent development, these figures are particularly encouraging when you look at Arc Raiders, the current top dog in the extraction shooter space, and the game that stole Marathon’s thunder last year when the two of them were being promoted by their publishers. Marathon, of course, got delayed out of 2025, which allowed Arc Raiders to launch first. It, of course, ended up proving that extraction shooters can be mainstream hits.

Like Marathon, Arc Raiders hosted its own server slam just a few days before its launch. That open test attracted 189,668 concurrent players at its peak, which is not that far off from Marathon’s so far.

According to recent reports, assuming positive word of mouth continues, more players are bound to jump in over the weekend and perhaps get Marathon to match or even exceed Arc Raiders’ record. At any rate, this is good news for beleaguered Bungie and points to what could be a big launch.

Marathon arrives March 5 on PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X/S.

#156399. Harvard’s tiny UV light chip could help shrink quantum computers

Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Harvard’s tiny UV light chip could help shrink quantum computers

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1174 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ultraviolet (UV) light is already essential to a wide range of modern technologies.
  • However, shrinking UV light sources to fit on a chip has presented a significant engineering challenge.
  • In a recent development, now, a Harvard-led research team has demonstrated a microscopic photonic device that produces approximately 120 times more UV power than previous comparable devices.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ultraviolet (UV) light is already essential to a wide range of modern technologies. Beyond its natural presence in sunlight, it is used to disinfect surfaces, make biological materials fluoresce, and manufacture computer chips through a process called photolithography. In the future, microscopic sources of UV light built directly into photonic chips could enable smaller quantum computers, ultra-precise atomic clocks, and other advanced technologies.

However, shrinking UV light sources to fit on a chip has presented a significant engineering challenge. Ultraviolet light rapidly loses power as it travels through optical waveguides, the tiny channels that carry light across a chip. This limitation has made it extremely difficult to develop compact UV sources with enough power for practical applications.

In a recent development, now, a Harvard-led research team has demonstrated a microscopic photonic device that produces approximately 120 times more UV power than previous comparable devices. The researchers, working in the laboratory of Marko Lončar, the Tiantsai Lin Professor of Electrical Engineering, achieved the breakthrough using a widely studied material called thin-film lithium niobate.

Published in Nature Communications, the findings establish lithium niobate as a promising platform for generating powerful ultraviolet light in compact devices while minimizing optical losses.

Turning Red Light Into Ultraviolet Light.

Rather than trying to deliver ultraviolet light directly through microscopic channels, the researchers designed a device that generates UV light from red light within the chip itself.

The approach relies on a process known as frequency upconversion. Inside the lithium niobate crystal, two photons of red light combine to produce a single ultraviolet photon with higher energy. Lithium niobate is particularly well suited to this process because of its exceptional ability to convert light from one frequency to another.

"Our group is perhaps best known for utilizing lithium niobate for photonic devices that operate at longer, infrared wavelengths -- closer to the realm of telecommunications signals," Lončar stated.

However, the team found that this transparent crystalline material, which has become increasingly key in integrated photonics, can also support light sources and guide light at much shorter wavelengths, including those in the ultraviolet range.

Sources indicate that "When people think about [thin-film lithium niobate], they don't think of it as a UV material, but we show that it is," stated co-first author Kees Franken, former research fellow in the Lončar lab. "We also show that there are some other nonlinear effects happening that we don't fully understand yet.".

A Fresh Technique Overcomes a Major Engineering Barrier.

The device uses optical waveguides, microscopic channels etched into the lithium niobate film that direct light through the chip in much the same way electrical wires carry current.

For red light to be efficiently converted into ultraviolet light, the orientation of regions within the crystal must be repeatedly reversed at precisely controlled intervals along the waveguide. This manufacturing process, called poling, is a specialized technique used in nonlinear optics.

One of the biggest challenges has been creating these patterns with accuracy at scales smaller than a micrometer across devices that extend for centimeters.

In a recent development, previous manufacturing methods required researchers to make an undesirable compromise. Poling the entire film before forming the waveguides made it difficult to correct manufacturing imperfections. Alternatively, creating the waveguides first reduced conversion efficiency because the electrodes were positioned too far away, allowing only part of the film to be successfully poled.

To eliminate this tradeoff, the Harvard team developed a technique they call "sidewall poling.".

Precision Engineering Dramatically Improves Light Conversion.

Instead of positioning the electrodes exclusively above the lithium niobate film, the researchers placed precisely patterned metal structures resembling tiny fingers directly alongside the etched waveguide. During fabrication, they applied a small voltage to permanently reverse the orientation of the crystal domains in a carefully controlled pattern.

It has been revealed that "The key idea was: could we just put the electrodes directly on the waveguide?" stated co-first author and former graduate student Soumya Ghosh. "It's a high-precision fabrication process to position the electrodes but requiring about 50-nanometer accuracy.".

This arrangement enabled the researchers to reverse the crystal domains throughout the entire cross section of the waveguide, allowing light traveling through the material to undergo much more efficient frequency conversion.

Industry observers note that the team could also fine-tune the spacing of the reversed crystal regions along the device. By incorporating existing "adapted poling" techniques previously developed in Lončar's laboratory and elsewhere, the researchers compensated for variations in the thickness of the lithium niobate film and the shape of the waveguide.

A 120-Fold Increase in Ultraviolet Power.

The resulting device generated 4.2 milliwatts of ultraviolet power directly on the chip at a wavelength of 390 nanometers. That represents approximately 120 times the output power achieved by the best previous thin-film lithium niobate devices operating in this wavelength range.

Earlier experiments using the material generated only tens of microwatts of UV power. Although those results demonstrated that the approach was scientifically feasible, the output was too low to support practical applications.

The substantial increase in power could be particularly valuable for trapped-ion quantum computers. These machines use electrically charged atoms to store and process quantum information. Many of the specific atomic energy transitions required to operate them involve light in the near-ultraviolet portion of the spectrum.

"If you want a scalable quantum computer that isn't the size of a truck, you need to scale everything down to the chip level, and this includes the light sources," Franken mentioned.

Sources indicate that the technology could also benefit ultra-precise atomic clocks and environmental monitoring systems. According to the researchers, the same range of ultraviolet wavelengths is well suited to compact sensors designed to closely monitor greenhouse gases and other atmospheric pollutants.

Franken and Ghosh attribute the breakthrough partly to the collaborative structure of Lončar's laboratory, where researchers carry out every stage of device development in one place, including theoretical research, engineering design, cleanroom fabrication, and optical testing.

"The hands-on intuition that we gained for how to make a device, while also keeping the zoomed-out view of what this device is for, and how we were going to characterize it -- that's a massive part of what enabled this project for us," Ghosh noted.

In a recent development, "Milliwatt-level UV generation using sidewall poled lithium niobate" was further co-authored by C.C. Rodrigues, J. Yang, C.J. Xin, S. Lu, D. Witt, G. Joe, G.S. Wiederhecker, and K.-J. Boller.

In a recent development, U.S. federal funding for the project came from the following sources: Department of the Air Force grant No. FA9453-23-C-A039; Office of Naval Research grant No. N00014-22-C-1041/VAS-21-0001; NASA grant No. 80NSSC22K0262 and 80NSSC23PB442; and National Science Foundation grants ERC EEC-1941583 and OMA-2137723.

Materials provided by Harvard John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences. Original written by Anne J. Manning. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

I would hope that this isn't a case of Embracer cutting staff in the misguided hope that they can just be replaced with the use of genAI, but who can say. Solidarity to those affected, who I hope can find new work soon.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the Sims 4 has officially entered into its paid mods era.
  • According to recent reports, the two new features will arrive first on PC and Mac, starting March 17.
  • In a recent development, the Maker Program is a way for community creators to get their work out there, and profit from it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the Sims 4 has officially entered into its paid mods era. Developer Maxis revealed The Sims Maker Program, and The Sims 4 Marketplace - two new destinations to publish, and discover new add-on content.

According to recent reports, the two new features will arrive first on PC and Mac, starting March 17. PlayStation and Xbox players will receive them over the next couple of months, which is very much in line with how other franchises have rolled out their own paid mods systems.

In a recent development, the Maker Program is a way for community creators to get their work out there, and profit from it. The content they create will end up on the Marketplace, where other players can browse it, and pay for it if they want to use it in their game.

According to recent reports, created content will be available across all platforms. All previous packs The Sims 4 players should be familiar with will move to the Marketplace, too: once the feature introduces, this is where you’re going to find Expansion Packs, Game Packs, Stuff Packs, Kits, and other official additions created by Maxis.

Alongside this, the game is also introducing a upcoming virtual currency - Moola - which is what you’re going to use to purchase Maker Packs, as well as Sims 4 Kits in the Marketplace. A portion of your purchase will go to the creator (roughly 30%) of what you buy.

It is worth noting, however, that you’ll still be able to buy Expansion Packs, Game Packs, and Stuff Packs without having to purchase Moola, or go through the Marketplace. Kits are the only items that will no longer be available on the existing PC/console storefronts. Moola comes in the usual denominations you’ve seen a hundred items in other games’ in-game shops.

In a recent development, in order to start creating custom content and publishing it on the Marketplace, you’ll need to first be accepted into the program. Once that’s done, you’ll be able to directly publish your content on the Marketplace.

Sources indicate that in the blog post announcing the latest features, Maxis said that creators will have control over the price of their content, and how it's packaged. These are referred to as Maker Packs, which can include Create-a-Sim or Build/Buy items.

You can apply to become a Maker from March 5. Once accepted, you’ll also get access to the Maker Suite, which is what you’re going to use to test your work to ensure it runs smoothly on the different platforms, and eventually publish it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that as AI usage during game development and discussions surrounding it become more prominent, Ubisoft has been taking a firm stance on embracing it. But according to the company itself, the usage of such tools is more like a suggestion than a rule to be strictly followed.

According to a report yesterday from Vertical Slice, the company has been enforcing generative AI usage across its development teams in order to increase productivity and enhance the project in general. And if you choose not to implement it, you would have to justify your choice.

However, Ubisoft has now responded to the original reporting, stating that while they do encourage AI usage across all production stages, it doesn’t mean that they require every single project to implement it, as they still need to be added only when it actually makes sense.

It has been revealed that the original version of Vertical Slice’s report states that, after speaking with various employees (who chose to remain anonymous due to possible backlash), Ubisoft is looking forward to increasing its gen-AI usage across all titles. If they choose not to use it, they have to detail the reasons for their choice. Otherwise, their ideas wouldn’t be approved to be worked on.

The report came out days after Ubisoft confirmed that their newest studio, Motherbrain, would be an AI-focused studio, being an important part of their “upcoming operating model”. The announcement also came days after over 160 staff members were let go from their positions in Canada-based studios.

According to Ubisoft, they are simply encouraging their “teams to explore where AI can be useful and bring value to their work.”.

While it all seems daunting and terrifying, the studio decided to step up to clarify exactly what it all means. According to Ubisoft, they are simply encouraging their “teams to explore where AI can be useful and bring value to their work,” and ensuring that no employee is being silently forced to implement gen-AI in their work.This aligns with a claim from one of the employees Vertical Slice spoke with. According to them, while they aren’t outright mandated to use AI in their projects, the company has fully decided to implement it whenever they have the chance.

Sources indicate that while "AI psychosis" has been a thing for a while, it’s undeniable that the existence of generative tools has greatly shifted the industry and its inner workings in just a couple of years. From waves of layoffs followed by AI-pilled initiatives and the implementation of disclaimers about its usage on official game store pages, it’s hard not to be alarmed by all of these signals.

Recent findings suggest that ubisoft has been a huge player in these changes. The newly introduced Motherbrain studio is a byproduct of Teammates, an AI experiment from last year. This AI-powered demo uses the tool to mold your experience according to your voice and actions, as NPCs will react to your commands and, as stated on their official site, “allow players to experience the story in their own way”.

With all of these fresh advances in mind, it’s not unexpected to see such a posture from the tech giant. However, it doesn’t mean they should be free of criticism when it's due. It’s hard not to associate all of the previously mentioned layoffs (which have been ever more common in the industry) with the increasing fear of being replaced by AI.

Another Ubisoft employee also mentioned feeling “cornered by generative AI all the time” since the recent attitude shift from the higher-ups, implying that some pressure over AI usage does exist inside the manufacturer.

According to recent reports, this doesn’t mean that Ubisoft’s own statement is incorrect. It could simply be a different way of perceiving attitudes and decisions taken by the company. But with so many AI-related incidents across the industry, such as the recent wave of AI game copies, it’s hard not to be worried about the future of gaming.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • As reported by Reuters and The Game Business, the body ruled that the lawsuit - brought by Alex Neill on behalf of folks who bought digital games on PlayStation between August 2016 and February 2026 - failed to establish that Sony had infringed competition law.
  • According to recent reports, the lawsuit claimed that PlayStation's dominant position when it comes to selling digital games on its platforms via the PlayStation Store subjected consumers to "excessive and unfair prices", as a result of terms and a 30% commission fee levied against developers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that it's a joyous day for lawyers representing plucky little game and console makers Sony. A UK class action lawsuit which accused the company of using the PlayStation Store's dominant market position to fuel "excessive and unfair" prices for digital games has been dismissed in its entirety by the Competition Appeal Tribunal in London.

As reported by Reuters and The Game Business, the body ruled that the lawsuit - brought by Alex Neill on behalf of folks who bought digital games on PlayStation between August 2016 and February 2026 - failed to establish that Sony had infringed competition law.

According to recent reports, the lawsuit claimed that PlayStation's dominant position when it comes to selling digital games on its platforms via the PlayStation Store subjected consumers to "excessive and unfair prices", as a result of terms and a 30% commission fee levied against developers. Neill and co argued owning a PlayStation traps game buyers within a competitionless ecosystem, thereby impacting their ability to seek out a better deal.

Sources indicate that it's quite similar to the arguments which have been made against Valve in similar lawsuits concerning the Steam overlords' dominance over the PC game buying space, though a key distinction is that there is some competition on PC via the likes of the Epic store and GOG. How effective some of that competition can be in practice is a different kettle of fish, but the options are there.

According to recent reports, in a judgement that could potentially factor into the responses to any similar lawsuits against Valve or other PC storefronts going forwards, the tribunal ruled that Sony compete in a wider ‘systems market’ against Xbox, Nintendo and PC, with PlayStation having no legal duty under competition law to allow third-party stores onto their platform as competition closer to home. The latter the tribunal noted would be expensive, complex and come with potential security ramifications.

As if that wasn't enough, the body ruled that as far as the pricing being unfair went, Neill hadn't proven that Sony’s profit margins were excessive and declared there was no evidence the presence of rival storefronts on PlayStation would've seen prices come down. That's essentially the word NO written in the largest font possible on a sheet of paper the size of a table, then.

Sources indicate that every lawsuit's different, especially when filed in different countries, but if I was one of the other class action suits against Sony or another big game seller on the go at the moment, I'd maybe not be feeling so hot right now. On the other hand, perhaps seeing what the tribunal judged Neill not to have provided suffiencient evidence for might aid those other efforts in formulating their arguments ready to face the scrutiny of government bodies and corporate law-talkers.

Fnatic have signed Czech duelist Martin 'marteen' Pátek from Gentle Mates as their first upcoming player for VCT EMEA 2027. The London club are rebuilding after missing Champions for the first time in the team's history.

The London club’s new duelist is a player who hurt them badly in 2026. Colin ‘CoJo’ Johnson is listed as manager of the rebuilt roster.

The move still has one step left. Pley.gg listed the signing as still awaiting approval from Riot Games. The link is not fresh. Word of a verbal agreement between marteen and Fnatic emerged on 24 September. That was about a month before Gentle Mates released their whole roster.

Industry observers note that fnatic have already seen what the duelist can do. Gentle Mates came out on top when the two sides met at the 2026 EMEA Kickoff. That win sent Gentle Mates to Masters Santiago.

He led several stat categories in Santiago. Gentle Mates still went out 1–2 to AG and finished joint seventh to eighth. That result earned the team $35,000.

The rest of Gentle Mates’ year was quieter. The team failed to qualify for Masters London or Champions Shanghai. Marteen still finished VCT EMEA Stage 2 as the team’s top-rated player, with a rating of 1.23. Signing a player who stood out in a non-qualifying side suggests Fnatic are building around individual firepower.

In a recent development, fnatic’s own 2026 campaign ended earlier than planned. Joblife knocked them out with a 2–0 win in the VCT EMEA Stage 2 Play-Ins.

In a recent development, the signing follows a clear-out of long-serving players. Boaster had been with Fnatic since 3 February 2021. Alfajer arrived on 9 May 2022, and crashies on 11 December 2024.

Marteen’s own spell at Gentle Mates ran from 20 November 2025 to 25 October 2026. The two rosters are now tied together by the same transfer window.

Gentle Mates had already cleared their own decks. All five players on the active roster and both coaches were let go before the club’s first season as a VCT partner team.

For a British organisation, the swap leaves Fnatic’s identity in new hands. Boaster had been the longest-serving name in the departing group. Kaajak and Cloud are now the continuity, with marteen as the headline addition.

Fnatic do not need to qualify for the opening event. The club is one of eight EMEA partner teams for 2027, and each partner goes straight into Kickoff. Places at later events must be earned. Four teams from Open Qualifiers complete the field.

The first chance to see both rebuilt sides comes soon. The 2027 EMEA Kickoff, featuring 12 teams, runs from 14 January to 7 February 2027 at the Riot Games Arena in Berlin. Its top three teams will qualify for Masters Seoul, the first international event of the 2027 season.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, my Jason gets up at 7am every morning in GTA 6 and sips a cup of coffee while chatting with Lucia. Then he eats an apple, wanders onto the deck to work out, and comes back inside for a quick shower before plotting out his day. You've gotta be realistic, of course. There's no way he can make time to dive for Kenton's treasures and take on that next job with Donnie in an afternoon. But maybe there's time to swing by that fishing spot Cal mentioned and still get home in time to enjoy a few more scenes of domestic bliss.

I spent my first 20 or so hours playing GTA 6 like it was Stardew Valley rather than an action-packed crime epic, but that's OK by me, as I love the rhythm taking each fresh in-game day as its own little challenge. One night, scrolling social media while cuddled up with Lucia, I ran across a pilot looking for help up north, miles outside of Vice City. It'd be an all-day trip getting up there, but Jason had just gotten into meditation, and Lucia had mentioned a spot out on the edge of the swamp where he might be able to clear his head. Two birds with one stone.

After the usual morning routine, I hopped in the car and headed north, first toward that meditation spot. Surrounded by wildlife, this is the point where I realized you could use the binoculars to look around and study animals to add to the in-game compendium, and I spent more time than I care to admit simply enjoying the sights of the swamp and birdwatching. Oh, a great blue heron? Absolutely majestic.

Recent findings suggest that I almost had time left to make it up to that pilot job, but I got distracted by an abandoned dinosaur-themed minigolf course on the roadside. I spent hours trying to perfect each hole. By the time I realized how late it had gotten, the sun was already getting low. The twilight put one thought in my mind: "Shit, I'd better get home so I can hang out with Lucia before she goes to sleep.".

Industry observers note that but my Jason, clearly awakened to the power of nature by his birdwatching experience, ended up having greater duties than that of a wife guy. Along one of the winding roads that led back home, I heard such a commotion that I had to investigate – a prize pageant cow named Tootsie had escaped from her owner's trailer and was making a break for it.

It has been revealed that I headed her off with my car and got out to calmly talk her down, but as she finally settled I heard the words "save me" echoing in Jason's mind. Leading her back to the trailer, the owner is very grateful – even as he warns that Tootsie is destined for the slaughterhouse after her final run of shows. At this point, I realized who Jason was becoming. I let Tootsie run free, and when her owner got mad about it, I punched him in the face and stole his cowboy hat as he ran to his truck and drove away.

That alone might be enough to turn Jason into a hero of the animal rights movement, but the day was not yet done. As darkness settled in on the journey home, I was cruising along the highway on the outskirts of Vice City when I ran into a traffic jam. At first, I assumed this was just the last vestiges of rush hour traffic – but no, a group of activists was holding up an animal services truck which, they claimed, housed a wrongfully imprisoned bear.

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more.

According to recent reports, again, I knew what I had to do. I hopped out of my car, headed to the back door of the truck, and started punching it. (Look, I know I probably could've shot the lock off, but I wasn't about to fire a pistol on a busy highway and attract police attention.) As the traffic continued backing up for miles, the driver eventually panicked and hit the gas, running over one of the protesters in the process. As they screamed out for their fallen friend, I figured I better hop back in the car and drive off before things got any more heated.

It has been revealed that tragically, Lucia was already asleep by the time I got home, so I never got to see what Jason might've said about the day's ridiculous events. I did, however, get a little treat while scrolling Snapmatic in bed – an image of Tootsie looking so happy at the height of her pageant days. I hope, somewhere out in the wild, that she's living her best life.

Upsettingly, it is that time of the week again, as Take-Two are laying off staff at Firaxis, the developer behind Civilization and XCOM, only a little over a year the last time the studio suffered from layoffs. Firaxis are, notably, owned by Take-Two, the publisher of GTA 6 which comes out in, oh, two days time? Interesting timing, 'ey.

Word of the layoffs came from Bloomberg, who report that about 60 people are losing their jobs, apparently roughly a third of its staff. The studio's head, Heather Hazen, is also leaving. A spokesperson for 2K Games (the Take-Two label that manages Firaxis) shared a statement on the layoffs: "Firaxis is restructuring and recentering around the studio’s core strength - designing world class strategy games that have set the industry standard for the genre for the last 30 years.

"As part of these changes, the size of the studio is being reduced to focus on design, technology and the player experience, which means saying goodbye to talented colleagues who helped build Firaxis. These decisions are never easy, but they’re essential to build the next chapter of Firaxis." I don't feel personally confident in the idea that the only way to make a firm succeed is by laying a bunch of people off thereby making it much harder to make anything in the first place, especially in the lead-up to what will likely be the best selling game of the decade, but what do I know!

Bloomberg also report Firaxis have been working on a upcoming XCOM, which is yet to be declared, but the project has apparently had to contend with numerous development issues, missing a "significant milestone over the summer." This new XCOM game hasn't been cancelled at the very least, but anonymous sources that spoke with Bloomberg said it may have to deal with a shakeup due to the cuts. As always, solidarity with all those affected by this situation.
